## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlfleetstack{30}{100}{35}{25}{20}{15}{0}{0}
\end{marginfigure}

_Why does storage become the invisible bottleneck that prevents accelerators from reaching their potential?_

A training job can leave expensive accelerators idle even when its models fit in memory and its network has ample capacity. The next batch must arrive before computation needs it, and a saved checkpoint must remain usable when a worker fails. Storage becomes an invisible bottleneck because accelerator benchmarks often begin with data already in place, excluding the work needed to deliver inputs and preserve results. A pipeline that keeps one machine busy can fail when many workers compete for the same data source. A burst of checkpoint writes from one job can delay input reads for others, turning a local pause into lost progress across the fleet. Adding compute increases demand without necessarily increasing the shared system's ability to serve it. The consequences depend on the workload: compact training inputs may be easy to deliver even when saving model state dominates storage traffic, while larger samples can make continuous input delivery the limiting factor. Bringing data closer to the accelerator reduces some delays but adds staging traffic, capacity cost, and responsibility for preserving complete versions. A faster local save also provides little protection if the only copy disappears with the failed machine. Storage decisions therefore determine both how quickly the fleet advances and how much of that progress survives disruption. In C³ terms, storage design coordinates data movement and durable state so that available compute produces recoverable progress.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Compare storage demands of full-corpus training, checkpoint writes, and model serving across local and shared tiers
- Calculate input bandwidth and mean cache service time from workload demand and tier behavior
- Design prefetching, sharding, locality, and direct-storage paths that reduce fleet-scale accelerator starvation
- Specify storage commit and replay contracts that preserve correctness when distributed pipeline stages fail
- Select checkpoint staging and replication strategies that balance pause time, recovery risk, and storage cost
- Evaluate staging and tiering choices by total delivery cost, including transfer fees and idle accelerators
- Assess retrieval indexes and synthetic-data pipelines as storage workloads with distinct latency, consistency, and governance constraints

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CHAPTER START
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Chapter initialization and global imports
# │
# │ Why: Registers this chapter with the mlsys registry and provides shared
# │      imports for all subsequent calculation cells.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.physics import memory_from_params
from mlsysim.fmt import MarkdownStr, check, fmt, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_qty_int

# Resumable mixed-precision Adam checkpoint contract used throughout this chapter:
# FP16 model weights + FP32 master weights + two FP32 Adam moments. Gradients are
# recomputed after restore and are therefore excluded; scheduler/RNG/data-loader
# metadata is negligible at this scale.
CHECKPOINT_RESUME_BYTES_PER_PARAM = ReferenceStats.StorageTrainingCorpus.CheckpointBytesPerParameter
check(
    abs(CHECKPOINT_RESUME_BYTES_PER_PARAM.to(byte / param).magnitude - 14) < 1e-9,
    "Resumable Adam checkpoint contract must remain 14 bytes per parameter",
)
check(
    CHECKPOINT_RESUME_BYTES_PER_PARAM == BYTES_FP16 + BYTES_FP32 + BYTES_ADAM_STATE,
    "Checkpoint registry value must equal FP16 weights + FP32 master weights + two FP32 Adam moments",
)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: storage-fuel-line-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ STORAGE-COMPUTE GAP, DATASET FOOTPRINT, AND CHECKPOINT SCALE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-storage-fuel-line—opening quantitative framing of the
# │          HBM-vs-NVMe bandwidth gap and checkpoint data volume.
# │
# │ Goal:    Quantify the ~500x gap between HBM and NVMe, the compressed vs.
# │          tokenized corpus footprint, and the PB-scale checkpoint volume for
# │          a 30-day 175B training run.
# │ Show:    3.35 TB/s HBM, 7 GB/s NVMe, ~479x ratio, ~2,450 GB checkpoint,
# │          3 TB compressed corpus, 6 TB tokenized corpus, ~10.6 PB total
# │          checkpoint writes.
# │ How:     Read H100 HBM BW and NVMe BW from constants; compute checkpoint
# │          size from GPT-3 params × bytes per param; compute corpus variants
# │          from tokens × bytes/token; derive fleet total.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Hardware, Models
from mlsysim.physics import model_memory
from mlsysim.fmt import MarkdownStr, check, fmt, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_int, fmt_memory

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class StorageFuelLineContext:
    h_h100 = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    m_gpt3 = Models.Language.GPT3
    h100_bw = h_h100.memory.bandwidth
    nvme_bw_raw = Hardware.Cloud.H100.storage.bandwidth
    gpt3_params = m_gpt3.parameters
    training_tokens = ReferenceStats.StorageTrainingCorpus.TrainingTokens
    compressed_text = ReferenceStats.StorageTrainingCorpus.CompressedSource
    token_id_bytes = ReferenceStats.StorageTrainingCorpus.TokenIdBytes
    training_window = ReferenceStats.StorageTrainingCorpus.TrainingWindow
    checkpoint_interval = ReferenceStats.StorageTrainingCorpus.CheckpointInterval
    bytes_per_param_ckpt = CHECKPOINT_RESUME_BYTES_PER_PARAM
    bw_ratio_val = (h100_bw / nvme_bw_raw).to("").magnitude
    ckpt_total = memory_from_params(gpt3_params * param, bytes_per_param_ckpt)
    checkpoint_count_val = int((training_window / checkpoint_interval).to("").magnitude)
    ckpt_fleet_total = ckpt_total * checkpoint_count_val
    tokenized_text = training_tokens * token_id_bytes
    baseline_training = compressed_text + tokenized_text
    check(ckpt_total.to(GB).magnitude > 1000, "175B checkpoint must be > 1 TB")
    check(checkpoint_count_val == 4320, "30 days at 10-min checkpoint interval should be 4320")
    # Running cluster: 256 DGX H100 nodes, deliberately twice the 1,024-GPU reference.
    run_cluster = Systems.Clusters.Production_2K
    ref_scenario = Scenarios.DenseLLMPretrainingReference
    run_accels = run_cluster.total_accelerators
    run_nodes = run_cluster.count
    ref_accels = ref_scenario.system.total_accelerators
    ref_nodes = ref_scenario.system.count
    step_time = ReferenceStats.StorageTrainingCorpus.StepTime
    training_state_bpp = ReferenceStats.MixedPrecisionAdam.TrainingStateBytesPerParameter
    gradient_bpp = training_state_bpp - bytes_per_param_ckpt
    check(run_accels == 2 * ref_accels, "Running cluster is described as twice the reference cluster")
    check(
        abs(gradient_bpp.to(byte / param).magnitude - BYTES_FP16.to(byte).magnitude) < 1e-9,
        "Training state minus checkpoint must equal the FP16 gradient",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ───────────────────────────────────────
    run_accels_str = fmt_count(run_accels, commas=True)
    run_nodes_str = fmt_count(run_nodes, commas=True)
    ref_accels_str = fmt_count(ref_accels, commas=True)
    ref_nodes_str = fmt_count(ref_nodes, commas=True)
    training_tokens_str = fmt_tokens(training_tokens, scale="trillion", scale_style="word", precision=1, commas=False)
    step_time_ms_str = fmt_time(step_time, millisecond, precision=0, commas=False)
    ckpt_bpp_str = fmt_int(bytes_per_param_ckpt.to(byte / param).magnitude)
    training_state_bpp_str = fmt_int(training_state_bpp.to(byte / param).magnitude)
    gradient_bpp_str = fmt_int(gradient_bpp.to(byte / param).magnitude)
    checkpoint_interval_str = fmt_time(checkpoint_interval, minute, precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    checkpoint_interval_attr_str = fmt_time(checkpoint_interval, minute, precision=0, commas=False, style="word", attributive=True)
    training_window_attr_str = fmt_time(training_window, day, precision=0, commas=False, style="word", attributive=True)
    training_window_days_str = fmt_time(training_window, day, precision=0, commas=False, style="word")
    h100_bw_tb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(h100_bw, unit=TB / second, precision=2, commas=False)
    nvme_bw_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(nvme_bw_raw, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    bw_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(bw_ratio_val), precision=0, commas=True)
    compressed_text_tb_str = fmt_memory(compressed_text, unit=TB, precision=0, commas=False)
    tokenized_text_tb_str = fmt_memory(tokenized_text, unit=TB, precision=0, commas=False)
    baseline_training_tb_str = fmt_memory(baseline_training, unit=TB, precision=0, commas=False)
    ckpt_total_gb_str = fmt_memory(ckpt_total, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=True)
    ckpt_fleet_total_pb_str = fmt_memory(ckpt_fleet_total, unit=PB, precision=1, commas=True)
```

## The Fuel Line {#sec-storage-fuel-line}

The dense accelerator nodes of @sec-compute-infrastructure pack eight GPUs delivering petaFLOP/s of aggregate compute, and the InfiniBand fabrics of @sec-network-fabrics connect thousands of such nodes at hundreds of gigabits per second. Within the multi-tier fleet stack diagrammed in @fig-fleet-stack, data storage completes that physical foundation, staging training data, model weights, optimizer state, and intermediate checkpoints at the right distance from the accelerator. An engine without fuel is expensive sculpture. The engineering question is how to deliver that fuel fast enough that the accelerators of a training cluster never starve. This chapter poses that question on `{python} StorageFuelLineContext.run_nodes_str` eight-GPU nodes, `{python} StorageFuelLineContext.run_accels_str` accelerators in all, deliberately twice the `{python} StorageFuelLineContext.ref_accels_str`-GPU (`{python} StorageFuelLineContext.ref_nodes_str`-node) reference cluster used elsewhere in this book, because the larger fleet makes the pressure on shared storage easier to see. Every worked number for the 175B job uses this running cluster; a side scenario with a different workload or fleet size names its own scale where it appears.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/data_storage_c3_locator.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="C³ taxonomy triangle with vertices C1 (Compute), C2 (Communication), and C3 (Coordination), with the center Storage hub connecting all three axes."}

*Storage is the physical substrate spanning Compute ($C_1$), Communication ($C_2$), and Coordination ($C_3$).*
:::

Consider the running example for the storage analysis, an instance of Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3). A 175-billion parameter language model trains on `{python} StorageFuelLineContext.training_tokens_str` tokens of text: roughly `{python} StorageFuelLineContext.compressed_text_tb_str` in compressed source form, or `{python} StorageFuelLineContext.tokenized_text_tb_str` once represented as 4-byte token IDs. That token budget is set upstream of storage. Under the compute-optimal scaling results of @sec-vol2-intro-ai-scaling-laws-a043, the training-token count grows in proportion to parameter count, so each step up the model-size curve enlarges both the corpus the fleet must hold and the bytes each epoch must read. This corpus already sits below the compute-optimal allocation for a 175B-parameter model, so a compute-optimal run would raise both figures further. The run makes a single pass (one epoch) over this corpus, reading every selected token once in an order determined by the shuffle seed. No small "hot" subset dominates access. Meanwhile, each accelerator processes its local batch in roughly `{python} StorageFuelLineContext.step_time_ms_str`, then waits for the next. If storage cannot deliver data within that `{python} StorageFuelLineContext.step_time_ms_str` window, the accelerator sits idle, and the organization pays for silicon that produces heat instead of gradients.

The problem is deceptive because storage technology has improved substantially. Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) drives achieve `{python} StorageFuelLineContext.nvme_bw_gb_per_s_str` of sequential throughput, a figure that would have seemed out of reach a decade ago. An H100 moves data internally through high-bandwidth memory (HBM) at `{python} StorageFuelLineContext.h100_bw_tb_per_s_str`, roughly `{python} StorageFuelLineContext.bw_ratio_mult_str` the sequential bandwidth of a single NVMe drive. This ratio contrasts two tiers; it is not the rate at which storage must supply training inputs, because HBM bandwidth also carries repeated weight, activation, and tensor traffic during computation. The storage feed requirement is instead determined by the input-batch bytes each accelerator needs per iteration. Dividing those bytes by the compute window gives one worker's required delivery rate; summing across workers gives the fleet demand. That rate must be evaluated at each tier using the representation stored there, since compressed inputs and decoded tensors occupy different numbers of bytes. A hierarchy becomes useful when the durable source cannot meet that rate or its latency varies enough to interrupt computation. Faster tiers stage upcoming batches while the durable tier supplies capacity and preserves the source data.

The storage problem joins physics with economics. Physics favors the memory closest to the accelerator, which offers the highest bandwidth in the smallest capacity; economics favors shared storage, which pools far more capacity at lower cost per byte behind additional interfaces and service queues. Device technology, interconnects, and contention then determine the rate a particular consumer actually receives. The engineering task is to place and move data so that the accelerator receives each batch before it is needed. The resulting design problem is quantitative. It asks how fast each tier must be, how deep the pipeline must run, and which bytes are worth keeping close to the accelerator. Improving arithmetic throughput alone does not improve input delivery or checkpoint persistence. Those paths require their own bandwidth and latency budgets.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/data_storage_checkpoint_dominance.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="A two-rung ladder on a log scale: a tall blue rung for checkpoint writes towering over a tiny rung for per-epoch training data, showing checkpoints move over a thousand times more bytes than the dataset."}

*Over the run, checkpoint writes exceed one epoch of training-data reads by more than 1,000 times.*
:::

The canonical training-data footprint for this example is roughly `{python} StorageFuelLineContext.baseline_training_tb_str` across the hierarchy, combining the example's compressed corpus and tokenized shards. Additional shuffled or packed variants can raise the staging footprint, but the per-epoch training read over 4-byte token IDs is `{python} StorageFuelLineContext.tokenized_text_tb_str`. This chapter adopts one resumable mixed-precision Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) checkpoint contract: FP16 model weights, FP32 master weights, and two FP32 Adam moments, for `{python} StorageFuelLineContext.ckpt_bpp_str` bytes per parameter. This is the `{python} StorageFuelLineContext.training_state_bpp_str`-byte training state of @sec-compute-node-memory without its `{python} StorageFuelLineContext.gradient_bpp_str`-byte FP16 gradients, which are recomputed after restore, while scheduler, random-number-generator, and data-loader metadata are negligible at this scale. The resulting checkpoint is `{python} StorageFuelLineContext.ckpt_total_gb_str` every `{python} StorageFuelLineContext.checkpoint_interval_str`.

Over a `{python} StorageFuelLineContext.training_window_attr_str` training run on the `{python} StorageFuelLineContext.run_nodes_str`-node cluster, the storage system must deliver `{python} StorageFuelLineContext.tokenized_text_tb_str` of tokenized training data in the run's single epoch, absorb `{python} StorageFuelLineContext.ckpt_fleet_total_pb_str` of checkpoint writes, and stage model weights for evaluation runs. The sections that follow use this same contract for every checkpoint size, duration, retention total, and lifetime-write calculation.

Those numbers force the storage path. ML access patterns first invert the assumptions behind conventional storage systems; that inversion forces a hierarchy from HBM to cold archive; the hierarchy then requires a pipeline equation that sizes delivery, direct data paths that remove host copies, a checkpoint protocol for the dominant write traffic, and economics that decide which bytes belong at each tier. Serving-time model loading, retrieval indexes, and synthetic-data provenance are variations on the same fuel-line problem, and devices that move the boundaries between tiers close the chapter. In each workload, the storage system must place the right representation at the right distance before the accelerator asks for it.

## How ML Workloads Invert Storage Assumptions {#sec-storage-workload-inversion}

A database administrator moving to an ML infrastructure team would find that full-corpus pretraining workloads\index{Storage!workload inversion} invert many familiar storage design principles. The 175B running example makes the inversion concrete. Its training pass reads every selected token once, in shuffled order, and a run that makes several passes reshuffles the same corpus for each one. Under this scenario, no small "hot" subset dominates access. Fine-tuning, curriculum learning, hard-example mining, recommendation features, and retrieval do create skewed working sets, so the inversion is a workload property rather than a universal property of ML.

Transactional databases emphasize small random accesses and strong consistency. A database server might issue thousands of 4 KB reads per second to serve user queries. Storage designs for this workload combine caching algorithms that exploit repeated access, write-ahead logs that support recovery, and redundant array of independent disks (RAID)[^fn-raid-array-redundancy] configurations that trade capacity and performance for fault tolerance. The caching layers assume that recently accessed data will soon be accessed again. A full-corpus training scan breaks that assumption and changes the access pattern, while retaining the need to protect durable state.

[^fn-raid-array-redundancy]: **RAID (redundant array of independent disks)**\index{RAID!ML storage}: A Berkeley taxonomy of drive-combining strategies that trade redundancy, capacity, and I/O performance [@patterson1988raid]. RAID 0 stripes data without redundancy and can suit a disposable cache backed by a durable source. A drive failure then requires restaging; redundancy may still be worthwhile when that recovery cost or the required availability justifies it. Unreplicated checkpoints and sole dataset copies require a different durability contract.

Full-corpus pretraining inverts these assumptions when samples are packaged into sequential shards, allowing the pipeline to stream through datasets that span hundreds of terabytes. Individual accesses are large (megabytes rather than kilobytes) because models consume batches of images or text sequences. Immutable, versioned training shards avoid read-write conflicts during a run; checkpoint publication and live feature updates still require explicit consistency guarantees. Image and video workloads can demand hundreds of gigabytes per second for days or weeks; compact tokenized text can require much less input bandwidth even when checkpoint writes dominate total traffic. The mismatch between what storage was optimized for and what ML actually needs creates the **I/O wall**\index{I/O Wall!definition} (principle \ref{pri-io-wall}): when storage throughput cannot deliver training data as fast as accelerators consume it, GPUs idle regardless of their computational power. For bandwidth-heavy image and video inputs, that wall arrives when accelerator count grows faster than provisioned storage throughput, making the *data pipeline*, not the *model*, the limiting factor.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ How storage stalls surface as communication or coordination bottlenecks in the C$^3$ taxonomy is developed in @sec-appdx-c3-taxonomy-storage-substrate.
:::

A simple shard-assignment calculation shows how this bottleneck can emerge even when aggregate storage capacity looks ample.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: shard-contention-notebook
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SHARD CONTENTION PROBABILITY (NOTEBOOK)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: "The Thundering Herd: Shard Contention" .callout-notebook
# │
# │ Goal: Quantify the probability of multiple GPUs hitting the same storage shard.
# │ Show: contention_prob_pct ≈ 40%—inline in notebook result.
# │ How: Pr(at least one collision) = 1 - (Shards! / (Shards^Workers * (Shards-Workers)!)).
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_count
import math

class ShardContention:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    n_workers = 32  # GPUs in a data-parallel group
    n_shards = 1000  # Total shards in the dataset
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    # Classic birthday problem: Pr(no collision)
    # For small n_workers/K_shards, approx exp(-n_workers^2 / (2 K_shards))
    p_no_collision = math.exp(-(n_workers**2) / (2 * n_shards))
    p_collision = 1 - p_no_collision
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0.3 < p_collision < 0.5, f"Prob {p_collision:.2f} unexpected")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────
    sc_n_workers_str = fmt_count(n_workers, commas=False, label="worker")
    sc_n_shards_str = fmt(n_shards, precision=0, commas=False)
    sc_collision_prob_str = fmt_percent(p_collision, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
```

```{=latex}
\Needspace{18\baselineskip}
```

::: {#nbk-data-storage-thundering-herd-shard-contention .callout-notebook title="The thundering herd: Shard contention"}

**Problem**: A dataset is split into `{python} ShardContention.sc_n_shards_str` shards on a shared file system. If `{python} ShardContention.sc_n_workers_str` each pick a shard at random to start their next epoch, what is the probability that at least two GPUs "collide" on the same shard, creating a potential read hotspot? A shard collision does not imply a server collision unless the placement maps each shard to a distinct server.

**Math**:
This is a variant of the "Birthday Problem" in probability.

1. **Probability of No Collision**: $\approx e^{-n_{\text{workers}}^2/(2K_{\text{shards}})} = e^{-32^2/2{,}000} \approx 0.60$.
2. **Probability of Contention**: $1 - 0.60 = 40\%$.

**Systems insight**: With 32 workers and 1,000 shards, the `{python} ShardContention.sc_collision_prob_str` collision probability identifies a potential storage-shard hotspot\index{Shard contention!collision probability}. Whether that collision delays workers depends on shard placement, caching, and available service capacity. Coordinating shard assignments can reduce this source of tail latency\index{Tail latency!storage shard contention} when assignments spread demand across independently serving devices while preserving the intended sampling policy.

:::

Shard collisions are one runtime symptom of the I/O wall. Even without contention, a fixed input service time can become the limiting stage when compute becomes faster.

::: {#psp-data-storage-widening-i-o-wall .callout-perspective title="The moving I/O bottleneck"}

Hold the batch representation and storage path fixed while improving compute throughput. The batch now finishes sooner, leaving less time to deliver the next one. Prefetching can overlap delivery with execution, but it cannot overcome a sustained service-rate deficit. This compute-to-storage imbalance\index{I/O Wall!compute-storage divergence} does not imply that every larger model is input bound: a model that performs more computation on the same batch can instead give storage more time. The design must follow workload service times, not advertised peak-throughput trends.

:::

A normalized example isolates the effect. Suppose input delivery takes one quarter of the original compute time and overlaps perfectly with computation, so each batch takes the longer of the two service times. Doubling compute speed halves batch time, and quadrupling it halves batch time again, at which point compute and delivery take equal time. Beyond that point the pipeline is delivery bound. A sixteenfold faster accelerator still raises batch throughput only fourfold, and the remaining compute sits idle behind the input path. That plateau is an I/O wall\index{I/O Wall!hardware trend} for this workload and allocation. Faster storage, a more compact representation, or additional independent input paths can move it; deeper prefetching alone cannot.

The first inversion is access pattern\index{Access pattern!sequential vs. random}. Where database workloads exhibit *random access patterns* that benefit from seek-time optimization, full-corpus pretraining performs massive *sequential scans*. An epoch in the running example reads each selected sample once, in the order produced by shard and buffer shuffling. This pattern resembles video streaming more than database queries. Storage systems optimized for random IOPS[^fn-iops-throughput-tradeoff] waste capabilities on this workload, while systems optimized for sequential throughput excel. The distinction is quantitatively dramatic: a Gen4/Gen5 NVMe drive delivers roughly 7--14 GB/s for sequential reads, while small 4 KB random reads can fall near 0.5 GB/s, an order-of-magnitude to 30$\times$ penalty for the wrong access pattern. The penalty is even more severe on hard drives, where mechanical seek times impose a 100$\times$ throughput reduction for random access compared to sequential.

[^fn-iops-throughput-tradeoff]: **IOPS (Input/Output Operations Per Second)**\index{IOPS!ML irrelevance}: The metric that dominated storage procurement for decades because database workloads issue millions of small random reads. ML training inverts this priority: a pipeline streaming 256 MB shards sequentially needs sustained GB/s throughput, not per-operation speed. Provisioning storage by IOPS rating for an ML workload over-spends on random-access capability the pipeline never exercises.

The shuffling that ML training requires adds a complication rooted in the requirements of stochastic gradient descent. Stochastic gradient descent\index{SGD!shuffle requirement} requires that each mini-batch be drawn approximately uniformly from the training distribution; presenting samples in a correlated order (all samples from the same document, all images from the same class) biases the gradient estimates and slows or destabilizes convergence. True global shuffling would satisfy this requirement perfectly, but it requires random access across the entire dataset, destroying the sequential access pattern that storage hardware demands. Even for a multi-terabyte corpus, random per-sample seeks are I/O-prohibitive: a dataset of 1 trillion 4-byte tokens (about 4 TB) stored as individual elements on NVMe, accessed at random, would take hundreds to thousands of hours to read at the drive's random-read IOPS rate rather than about ten minutes of sequential streaming. The practical solution is therefore a compromise: shuffle the order of large data shards, then shuffle samples within each shard's local buffer. This achieves sufficient randomness for training convergence while preserving the sequential I/O pattern that storage hardware demands. The shard size determines the trade-off: larger shards provide more within-shard shuffle diversity but require more memory for the shuffle buffer.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-storage-workload-inversion
from mlsysim import Models, Hardware
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_qty_int, fmt_time

class StorageAccessPatternFacts:
    gpt3 = Models.Language.GPT3
    gpt3_params = gpt3.parameters
    training_tokens = ReferenceStats.StorageTrainingCorpus.TrainingTokens
    compressed_text = ReferenceStats.StorageTrainingCorpus.CompressedSource
    token_id_bytes = ReferenceStats.StorageTrainingCorpus.TokenIdBytes
    tokenized_text = training_tokens * token_id_bytes
    ckpt_total = gpt3_params * CHECKPOINT_RESUME_BYTES_PER_PARAM
    ckpt_node_count = Systems.Clusters.Production_2K.count  # the chapter's 256-node running cluster
    ckpt_shard = ckpt_total / ckpt_node_count
    ckpt_burst = ckpt_shard * ckpt_node_count
    checkpoint_interval = ReferenceStats.StorageTrainingCorpus.CheckpointInterval
    check(abs(ckpt_burst.to(TB).magnitude - ckpt_total.to(TB).magnitude) < 0.01, "Burst write volume must equal checkpoint size")
    rollout_replicas = 100  # scenario assumption: serving replicas updated in one rollout
    rollout_weights = memory_from_params(gpt3_params, BYTES_FP16 / param)
    rollout_total = rollout_replicas * rollout_weights
    check(abs(rollout_total.to(TB).magnitude - 35) < 1e-6, "100 replicas of 350 GB FP16 weights should total 35 TB")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    gpt3_params_b_str = fmt_params(gpt3_params, scale="B", precision=0, commas=False)
    tokenized_text_tb_str = fmt_memory(tokenized_text, unit=TB, precision=0, commas=False)
    compressed_text_tb_str = fmt_memory(compressed_text, unit=TB, precision=0, commas=False)
    ckpt_total_gb_str = fmt_qty_int(ckpt_total, GB)
    checkpoint_interval_min_str = fmt_time(checkpoint_interval, minute, precision=0, commas=False, style='word')
    ckpt_node_count_str = fmt_count(ckpt_node_count, commas=True, label="node")
    ckpt_shard_gb_str = fmt_qty_int(ckpt_shard, GB, commas=False)
    ckpt_burst_tb_str = fmt_memory(ckpt_burst, unit=TB, precision=1, commas=False)
    rollout_replicas_str = fmt_int(rollout_replicas)
    rollout_total_tb_str = fmt_memory(rollout_total, unit=TB, precision=0, commas=False)
```
The second inversion is working set size\index{Working set size!full-corpus training}. Traditional applications exhibit temporal locality\index{Locality!temporal}: a web server repeatedly accesses popular pages, and a cache holding the top 10 percent of content serves 90 percent of requests. In the chapter's full-corpus pretraining scenario, the `{python} StorageAccessPatternFacts.tokenized_text_tb_str` serialized corpus has no "popular" token range; each selected token is consumed once per epoch. A cache of any practical size holds only a small fraction of the corpus, and most samples are effectively "cold" when accessed. This access pattern makes traditional recency caching much less effective. A least recently used (LRU)[^fn-lru-eviction-failure] cache can approach a 0 percent hit rate for a cyclic scan larger than the cache. With independently reshuffled epochs, cross-epoch hits are low but nonzero and depend on the cache fraction and sample order.

[^fn-lru-eviction-failure]: **LRU (Least Recently Used)**\index{LRU!ML failure mode}: LRU is effective when recently accessed data is likely to be accessed again soon; a cyclic full-dataset scan larger than the cache can evict each sample before its next access and drive the hit rate toward zero. Independent reshuffling changes the boundary behavior because some samples retained from the end of one epoch may be reused before eviction in the next, so the hit rate depends on the cache-to-dataset ratio and ordering rather than being universally zero. Teams should measure this reuse before allocating DRAM that could otherwise serve as prefetch buffers.

Other training policies create different locality. Multi-task or curriculum learning\index{Curriculum learning!data locality}, hard-example mining, and filtered sampling access some subsets more frequently during particular phases. This temporary working set lets the NVMe tier exploit locality. Large-scale pretraining jobs that repeatedly scan a fixed corpus remain the scenario for the hierarchy derived here; systems serving another sampling policy should measure its reuse distribution before adopting the same cache design.

The third inversion is write pattern\index{Write pattern!bursty writes}. Transactional systems generate continuous streams of small writes, each immediately durable. ML systems generate occasional massive writes when saving checkpoints. A `{python} StorageAccessPatternFacts.gpt3_params_b_str` parameter model checkpoint, including optimizer state, occupies roughly `{python} StorageAccessPatternFacts.ckpt_total_gb_str`. Saving it every `{python} StorageAccessPatternFacts.checkpoint_interval_min_str` generates concentrated bursts that saturate bandwidth for seconds, followed by long idle periods. These synchronized bursts, called checkpoint storms\index{Checkpoint Storm!write bursts} and defined formally in definition \ref{dfn-data-storage-checkpoint-storm}, must be absorbed by the shared file system without disrupting ongoing training reads. The bursty write pattern is particularly challenging because all nodes in the cluster write their checkpoint shards simultaneously. If `{python} StorageAccessPatternFacts.ckpt_node_count_str` each write `{python} StorageAccessPatternFacts.ckpt_shard_gb_str`, the parallel file system receives `{python} StorageAccessPatternFacts.ckpt_burst_tb_str` of writes in a single burst, which blocks training if the job writes synchronously to that tier. Local staging and asynchronous replication can shorten this pause, as @sec-storage-checkpointing develops. When checkpoint and gradient traffic share one fabric, traffic isolation also keeps the burst from delaying the job's collectives.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Traffic isolation and quality-of-service mechanisms are established in @sec-network-fabrics-qos.
:::

The fourth inversion is subtler. The read/write ratio shifts dramatically by lifecycle phase. During the intervals between checkpoints, the input pipeline reads continuously. Across a complete run, however, the read/write ratio depends on input size, epoch count, checkpoint size, and save frequency. The running language-model example produces far more checkpoint bytes than training-input bytes despite spending most of its time between saves. During data preprocessing, both reads and writes are heavy, and the access pattern more closely resembles a MapReduce job than a training loop: tokenization, deduplication, and shuffling scan the raw corpus once (large sequential reads), write intermediate artifacts (large sequential writes), and then scan those artifacts again for the next stage. A `{python} StorageAccessPatternFacts.compressed_text_tb_str` compressed text corpus typically expands to `{python} StorageAccessPatternFacts.tokenized_text_tb_str` of tokenized shards before the first training epoch begins, loading each storage tier differently from the read-only training phase that follows. No single storage configuration optimizes for all phases, which is why ML systems require a multi-tier hierarchy rather than a single storage technology.

A fifth inversion emerges when comparing training and inference workloads. *Training* reads datasets sequentially and writes checkpoints in bursts. Weight-resident *inference*, by contrast, performs one large model read at startup and then serves requests from HBM. Its storage challenge is cold-start latency: the time required to load a model when scaling up or recovering from failure. The binding constraint flips from sustained dataset throughput to a bulk read whose duration depends on which tier supplies the weights. Retrieval, state offload, and models larger than aggregate HBM create additional serving-time I/O, so this weight-resident case is a baseline rather than a universal inference pattern. @Sec-storage-inference derives the load times and connects that baseline to the retrieval workload that follows.

When scaling from a single user to thousands of concurrent inference requests, the storage challenge shifts from a single-stream throughput problem to a massive fan-out distribution problem. A serving cluster with `{python} StorageAccessPatternFacts.rollout_replicas_str` replicas of our 175B parameter model holds `{python} StorageAccessPatternFacts.rollout_total_tb_str` of FP16 model weights across the cluster. When a new model version is deployed (a model rollout\index{Model rollout!storage bandwidth}), all `{python} StorageAccessPatternFacts.rollout_replicas_str` replicas must be updated, triggering a `{python} StorageAccessPatternFacts.rollout_total_tb_str` data distribution event that must complete within minutes to minimize serving disruption. This is analogous to the checkpoint storm\index{Checkpoint Storm!fan-out read comparison} in training but in reverse. Instead of many nodes *writing* to a central location simultaneously, many nodes are *reading* the same data simultaneously. The storage system must sustain this burst read bandwidth for model distribution while continuing to serve inference requests from the existing model version without degradation.

| **Workload Pattern**       |          **Traditional Assumption**          |                             **ML Reality**                            |
|:---------------------------|:--------------------------------------------:|:---------------------------------------------------------------------:|
| **Access pattern**         |                Random access                 |                          Sequential streaming                         |
| **Working set**            | Fits in cache, with strong temporal locality |      Exceeds all cache levels; low locality in full-corpus scans      |
| **Write pattern**          |           Continuous small writes            |                          Bursty large writes                          |
| **Read/write ratio**       |                   Balanced                   |             Phase-dependent (read-only to write-dominated)            |
| **Training vs. inference** |      One access pattern for all phases       | Corpus streaming in training; bulk model loads and fan-out in serving |

: **ML Workloads Invert Traditional Storage Assumptions**: The five inversions of full-corpus training and serving. Where databases optimize for random IOPS with cacheable working sets, ML training streams sequentially through datasets that exceed all cache levels and writes state in bursts, its read/write balance shifts by lifecycle phase, and serving replaces dataset streaming with bulk model loads. {#tbl-storage-assumptions}

@Tbl-storage-assumptions collects the five inversions, and together they reduce to one procurement rule, which is to optimize for streaming reads and bursty writes rather than database-style random IOPS. An organization provisioning storage for ML based on database-era heuristics will over-invest in random IOPS for sequential training shards, under-invest in the sustained bandwidth those shards require, and fail to account for the bursty write patterns that checkpointing creates.

::: {#chk-data-storage-storage-workload-analysis .callout-checkpoint title="Storage workload analysis"}

You are designing the storage subsystem for a new ML training cluster with 512 GPUs. The primary workload will train large language models on a 10 TB text dataset.

- [ ] **Database heuristics**: use the five storage workload inversions to name at least three database optimization strategies that would be counterproductive for this workload.
- [ ] **Epoch reads**: calculate the total data volume read when each training epoch reads the full 10 TB dataset once and the cluster trains for 100 epochs, then compare it to a typical database workload.
- [ ] **Checkpoint bandwidth**: calculate the minimum write bandwidth required when the model saves a 500 GB checkpoint every 15 minutes and each save must complete within 30 seconds.
- [ ] **Write duty cycle**: calculate the percentage of time the storage system spends in "write mode" vs. "read mode" under bursty checkpoints every 15 minutes.

:::

Which storage tier can keep accelerators fed depends on workload demand, not on a model's parameter count. The required rate is the aggregate input bytes consumed during a delivery window divided by that window, and demand above a tier's allocated service rate cannot be sustained by prefetching alone. A larger model need not require a higher input rate, because representation, batch size, parallelism, and compute time jointly determine it; @sec-storage-pipeline-equation turns that dependence into a sizing equation. Adding clients can raise the aggregate service a shared tier provides, while contention lowers the share available to any one job.

The practical consequence for the running example is stark. The `{python} StorageFuelLineContext.training_tokens_str` tokens of training data produce roughly `{python} StorageAccessPatternFacts.tokenized_text_tb_str` of sequential token-ID reads per epoch, even though the compressed source corpus is only `{python} StorageAccessPatternFacts.compressed_text_tb_str`. Stored as one file per sample, the corpus would spend its storage service on file opens rather than payload bytes, a metadata request rate rather than a byte rate that @sec-storage-tier3-pfs develops as the small file problem. Preprocessing it into large sequential shards [@aizman2019] amortizes the fixed cost of open, seek, and close across many tokens, reducing metadata demand without changing the required payload rate; @sec-storage-data-formats compares the shard formats that make this packaging work. Where those shards should live, and how close to the accelerator, is the question the storage hierarchy answers.

## The ML Storage Hierarchy {#sec-storage-hierarchy}

A system architect must organize storage to serve workloads that simultaneously demand terabytes-per-second bandwidth for computation, petabyte-scale capacity for datasets, and durable checkpoints. No single technology satisfies all three requirements. HBM supplies high local bandwidth at limited capacity; object storage pools durable capacity, but delivery depends on its service and client paths. A multi-tier hierarchy\index{Tiered storage!hierarchy} combines these resources rather than requiring one technology to meet every demand. Each tier offers a different balance of bandwidth\index{Bandwidth!storage hierarchy}, latency\index{Latency!storage hierarchy}, capacity, and cost. The hierarchy extends the familiar processor memory hierarchy\index{Storage hierarchy!extended memory hierarchy} across nodes. The new fleet-level decision is how local staging reduces demand on shared storage while preserving a durable, consistently versioned source. @Tbl-storage-hierarchy-merged compares the resources at their stated device, node, and service scopes.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/data_storage_bandwidth_cliff.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Three stacked horizontal bars on a log scale, longest at top: HBM at 3.35 TB/s, host DRAM at 200 GB/s, and NVMe at 7 GB/s, showing bandwidth dropping sharply across the top three storage tiers."}

*Bandwidth drops roughly 479$\times$ across the top three tiers, from HBM to local NVMe.*
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @tbl-storage-hierarchy-merged and bandwidth cliffs
from mlsysim import Hardware
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_bandwidth, fmt_time

class StorageHierarchyTable:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    nvme_latency = Hardware.Tech.Storage.NvmeGen4.latency
    host_dram_bw = Hardware.Tech.Storage.HostDram.bandwidth
    nvme_bw = Hardware.Tech.Storage.NvmeGen4.bandwidth
    pfs_bw = Systems.Storage.PfsOneTbPerSecond.bandwidth
    hbm_cost = Infrastructure.Pricing.Storage.HbmEquivalentPerGb.rate
    dram_cost = Infrastructure.Pricing.Storage.HostDramLowPerGb.rate
    nvme_cost = Infrastructure.Pricing.Storage.NvmeLowPerTbMonth.rate
    pfs_cost = Infrastructure.Pricing.Storage.ParallelFileSystemPerTbMonth.rate
    object_cost = Infrastructure.Pricing.Storage.S3StandardLowPerTbMonth.rate
    archive_cost = Infrastructure.Pricing.Storage.GlacierStandardPerTbMonth.rate

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ───────────────────────────────────────
    nvme_bw_low_gb_str = fmt_int(nvme_bw.to(GB / second).magnitude)  # lower bound of a "7--25 GB/s" range
    pfs_bw_tb_str = fmt_int(pfs_bw.to(TB / second).magnitude)  # lower bound of a "1+ TB/s" figure
    hbm_cost_str = fmt_usd(hbm_cost, per="GB", precision=0, approx=True)
    dram_cost_str = fmt_usd(dram_cost, per="GB", precision=0, approx=True)
    nvme_cost_str = fmt_usd(nvme_cost, per="GB/month", precision=2, commas=False, approx=True)
    pfs_cost_str = fmt_usd(pfs_cost, per="GB/month", precision=2, commas=False, approx=True)
    object_cost_str = fmt_usd(object_cost, per="GB/month", precision=2, commas=False, approx=True)
    archive_cost_str = fmt_usd(archive_cost, per="GB/month", precision=3, commas=False, approx=True)
    h100_bw_tb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(Hardware.Cloud.H100.memory.bandwidth, unit=TB / second, precision=2, commas=False)
    nvme_latency_us_str = fmt_time(nvme_latency, microsecond, precision=0, commas=False)
    host_dram_bw_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(host_dram_bw, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
```

| **Storage Tier**         | **Typical Capacity** |                         **Bandwidth**                          |                      **Latency**                      |                    **Illustrative Cost Basis**                    |
|:-------------------------|:--------------------:|:--------------------------------------------------------------:|:-----------------------------------------------------:|:-----------------------------------------------------------------:|
| **GPU HBM**              |        80 GB         |     `{python} StorageHierarchyTable.h100_bw_tb_per_s_str`      |                        ~100 ns                        |   `{python} StorageHierarchyTable.hbm_cost_str` acquisition cost  |
| **Host DRAM**            |     512 GB--2 TB     |   `{python} StorageHierarchyTable.host_dram_bw_gb_per_s_str`   |                        ~100 ns                        |  `{python} StorageHierarchyTable.dram_cost_str` acquisition cost  |
| **Local NVMe SSD**       |       4--30 TB       |  `{python} StorageHierarchyTable.nvme_bw_low_gb_str`--25 GB/s  | ~`{python} StorageHierarchyTable.nvme_latency_us_str` |     `{python} StorageHierarchyTable.nvme_cost_str` provisioned    |
| **Parallel File System** |       100+ PB        | `{python} StorageHierarchyTable.pfs_bw_tb_str`+ TB/s aggregate |                         ~1 ms                         | `{python} StorageHierarchyTable.pfs_cost_str` provisioned/service |
| **Object Storage**       |   Very large pool    |                       100 GB/s aggregate                       |                         ~50 ms                        |      `{python} StorageHierarchyTable.object_cost_str` service     |
| **Archive/Cold Storage** |   Very large pool    |                             1 GB/s                             |                    Minutes to hours                   |     `{python} StorageHierarchyTable.archive_cost_str` service     |

: **Extended Memory Hierarchy for ML Systems**: HBM bandwidth is per accelerator, host DRAM and local NVMe are per node, and parallel-file-system and object-storage figures are aggregate service rates. These different scopes are not directly comparable tier ratios; divide shared bandwidth among active clients and account for each client path before sizing prefetching and caching. Memory costs are acquisition dollars per GB, while storage costs are recurring dollars per GB-month; comparing them requires an explicit amortization period and utilization assumption. {#tbl-storage-hierarchy-merged}

One reading of @tbl-storage-hierarchy-merged is worth flagging: HBM's advantage over host DRAM is *bandwidth*, not *latency*. Random-access latency for both technologies sits in the ~80--150 ns range; HBM achieves its bandwidth lead (10--20$\times$) through thousands of parallel traces on a silicon interposer and 3D stacking, not faster cells. The latency cliff between adjacent tiers only opens up at NVMe and below, where the physical distance from the accelerator grows from millimeters to meters.

The storage hierarchy model (principle \ref{pri-storage-hierarchy}) governs storage tiering and pipeline design. The local tiers exchange bandwidth for capacity, while shared tiers aggregate many devices and expose a different client path. The per-client bandwidth depends on allocation and contention rather than a fixed factor between tiers. Data format choices, caching strategies, prefetch buffer sizing, and tiering policies all exist to manage the movement of data upward through the hierarchy so that the accelerator never starves.
```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @tbl-storage-hierarchy-merged and bandwidth cliffs
from mlsysim import Hardware
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_memory, fmt_multiple, fmt_qty_int

class StoragePyramidContext:
    training_tokens = ReferenceStats.StorageTrainingCorpus.TrainingTokens
    compressed_text = ReferenceStats.StorageTrainingCorpus.CompressedSource
    token_id_bytes = ReferenceStats.StorageTrainingCorpus.TokenIdBytes
    h100_bw = Hardware.Cloud.H100.memory.bandwidth
    host_dram_bw = Hardware.Tech.Storage.HostDram.bandwidth
    nvme_bw = Hardware.Tech.Storage.NvmeGen4.bandwidth
    raid0_drive_count = Systems.Storage.LocalNvmeGen4_7T68x4.devices_per_node
    raid0_bw = raid0_drive_count * nvme_bw
    pfs_bw = Systems.Storage.PfsOneTbPerSecond.bandwidth
    pfs_nodes = Systems.Clusters.Production_2K.count  # the chapter's 256-node running cluster
    pfs_per_node_bw = pfs_bw / pfs_nodes
    tokenized_text = training_tokens * token_id_bytes
    hbm_host_dram_ratio_val = (h100_bw / host_dram_bw).to("").magnitude
    dram_nvme_ratio_val = (host_dram_bw / raid0_bw).to("").magnitude
    raid0_pfs_ratio_val = (raid0_bw / pfs_per_node_bw).to("").magnitude
    check(6 < raid0_pfs_ratio_val < 8, "Local RAID-0 should be about 7x the per-node PFS share")
    check(
        round(pfs_per_node_bw.to(GB / second).magnitude) == round(Systems.Storage.PfsPerNodeShare.bandwidth.to(GB / second).magnitude),
        "Computed per-node PFS share must round to the registry per-node share used later in the chapter",
    )
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    compressed_text_tb_str = fmt_memory(compressed_text, unit=TB, precision=0, commas=False)
    tokenized_text_tb_str = fmt_memory(tokenized_text, unit=TB, precision=0, commas=False)
    h100_bw_tb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(h100_bw, unit=TB / second, precision=2, commas=False)
    host_dram_bw_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(host_dram_bw, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    raid0_bw_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(raid0_bw, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    hbm_host_dram_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(hbm_host_dram_ratio_val, precision=1, commas=False)
    dram_nvme_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(dram_nvme_ratio_val, precision=1, commas=False)
    raid0_drive_count_str = fmt_count(raid0_drive_count, commas=False)
    pfs_bw_tb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(pfs_bw, unit=TB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    pfs_nodes_str = fmt_count(pfs_nodes, commas=True)
    pfs_per_node_bw_gb_per_s_str = fmt_qty_int(pfs_per_node_bw, GB / second, commas=False)  # "roughly"; 3.9 GB/s rounds to the registry 4 GB/s share
    raid0_pfs_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(raid0_pfs_ratio_val), precision=0, commas=False)
```
The rest of the chapter numbers the six tiers by distance from the accelerator, from Tier 0 (HBM) through Tier 1 (host DRAM), Tier 2 (local NVMe), Tier 3 (parallel file system), and Tier 4 (object storage) to Tier 5 (archive). Distance alone hides an important distinction, because each tier's bandwidth figure describes a different scope: per accelerator, per node, or a shared service divided among its clients (@fig-storage-pyramid).

::: {#fig-storage-pyramid fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**ML storage hierarchy**: The six tiers of @tbl-storage-hierarchy-merged stacked by distance from the accelerator, with band width showing schematically how capacity grows toward the base; the table carries the numbers. The left brackets give the scope of each tier's bandwidth figure: per accelerator, per node, or an aggregate shared service that must be divided among its clients. The right column gives the physical path each byte travels to reach the accelerator. Blue memory tiers are bought per GB; green storage tiers are rented or provisioned per GB-month." fig-alt="A six-band pyramid, narrow at the top and wide at the base: GPU HBM, host DRAM, local NVMe, parallel file system, object storage, and archive. Brackets on the left group HBM as per accelerator, host DRAM and local NVMe as per node, and the bottom three as a shared service. A right-hand column lists each tier's path: millimeters over a silicon interposer, centimeters over the host memory bus, centimeters over PCIe lanes, meters over a switched network, kilometers of data-center fiber, and offline media."}

:::

The physical tiers diagrammed in @fig-storage-pyramid govern the trade-off among access distance, capacity, and cost. Shared services can aggregate more bandwidth than an individual local device, so the ordering is not a monotonic ranking of aggregate throughput. This trade-off is not arbitrary; it reflects the physics of data proximity. HBM sits on the same silicon interposer as the accelerator, connected by thousands of parallel traces measured in millimeters. Host DRAM connects to the CPU memory controller; transfers from host memory to the accelerator traverse the host-device interconnect. NVMe reaches across a circuit board via a PCIe connector. The parallel file system traverses meters of cable and network switches. Object storage may span kilometers of fiber between data centers. Distance, protocol overhead, and contention can increase access latency, while media technology and provisioning determine capacity cost. Distance is therefore a guide rather than a measurement; only the complete client path establishes all three properties for a given consumer.

The engineering challenge is to deliver each batch to HBM before the accelerator needs it. Return to the running example: the durable corpus lives in object storage (Tier 4) as a `{python} StoragePyramidContext.compressed_text_tb_str` compressed source copy plus `{python} StoragePyramidContext.tokenized_text_tb_str` of tokenized training shards, but the accelerator needs each batch in HBM (Tier 0) within `{python} StorageFuelLineContext.step_time_ms_str`. The chapter's reference design fixes one path between them. At job start, each node copies its share of the tokenized shards from object storage to its local NVMe (Tier 2); the single training epoch then reads from that local copy, prepares batches in host DRAM, and transfers them to HBM, while the parallel file system (Tier 3) holds checkpoints rather than training inputs. Streaming the shards directly from object storage, or serving them from a parallel file system, are the alternatives the chapter weighs against this design, and the hierarchy describes placement choices, not a requirement that every byte visit every level.

### Bandwidth cliffs between tiers {#sec-storage-bandwidth-cliffs}

The bandwidth ratios between adjacent tiers reveal the severity of each transition in the hierarchy, provided each rate is first converted to the scope bracketed in @fig-storage-pyramid, because a per-accelerator, per-node, or shared-service figure describes a different resource. Between HBM and host DRAM, the ratio is roughly `{python} StoragePyramidContext.hbm_host_dram_ratio_mult_str` (`{python} StoragePyramidContext.h100_bw_tb_per_s_str` vs. ~`{python} StoragePyramidContext.host_dram_bw_gb_per_s_str`). Between host DRAM and NVMe, the ratio is roughly `{python} StoragePyramidContext.dram_nvme_ratio_mult_str` (`{python} StoragePyramidContext.host_dram_bw_gb_per_s_str` vs. ~`{python} StoragePyramidContext.raid0_bw_gb_per_s_str` from a `{python} StoragePyramidContext.raid0_drive_count_str`-drive RAID-0). Between NVMe and a parallel file system, the ratio depends on the per-node allocation: if a `{python} StoragePyramidContext.pfs_bw_tb_per_s_str` aggregate parallel file system (PFS) serves `{python} StoragePyramidContext.pfs_nodes_str` nodes, each node receives roughly `{python} StoragePyramidContext.pfs_per_node_bw_gb_per_s_str`, a `{python} StoragePyramidContext.raid0_pfs_ratio_mult_str` reduction from the local RAID-0 stripe. Object-storage throughput likewise depends on the client path and allocation; there is no fixed ratio to a parallel file system.

As @sec-storage-fuel-line established, a cliff is not a feed requirement; the feed rate remains input-batch bytes divided by iteration time, summed over distinct consumers. What the cliffs decide is where buffering must sit. Along the chosen path, host DRAM can buffer prepared batches and NVMe can cache shards from shared storage. Each buffer must cover the delay of the tier below it while that tier sustains the consumption rate; durable repositories need not act as intermediate buffers.

The same hierarchy can be analyzed as a cache\index{Cache!effective service time} rather than as six isolated devices. If a request hits the hot tier with probability $h$, taking $T_{\text{hot}}$, and otherwise falls through to a colder tier, taking total end-to-end miss-path time $T_{\text{cold}}$ (including the failed hot-tier lookup), its mean service time is

$$
\mathbb{E}[T] = hT_{\text{hot}} + (1-h)T_{\text{cold}}.
$$ {#eq-storage-cache-service-time}

For fixed-size records served serially, the corresponding effective bandwidth is the record size divided by $\mathbb{E}[T]$. The arithmetic makes small miss rates consequential: with a 95 percent hit rate and a cold-tier access 100$\times$ slower than a hot-tier access, $\mathbb{E}[T]=5.95T_{\text{hot}}$, so the effective request rate is only about one-sixth of the all-hot rate. Concurrent requests and prefetching can overlap service, so this mean is a sizing baseline rather than a fleet-throughput or latency guarantee. Correlated misses or a heavy-tailed cold tier can drain the prefetch buffer even when the average satisfies the pipeline budget, so production designs must check a tail percentile and miss bursts as well as $\mathbb{E}[T]$.

The batch-volume arithmetic also explains why increasing cluster size creates storage pressure. Aggregate demand is each consumer's batch bytes divided by its compute window, summed over consumers, so at a fixed per-node rate it grows linearly with node count. The per-node rate itself spans orders of magnitude across data modalities, as text and image training on the running cluster show.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: data-storage-text-image-bandwidth
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TEXT VS IMAGE BANDWIDTH (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-data-storage-text-vs-image-bandwidth
# │
# │ Goal: Compute aggregate text and image storage bandwidth for a 2,048-GPU job.
# │ Show: 168 MB/s text; ~303 GB/s image; about 1,800x ratio.
# │ How: BW = GPUs × per-GPU batch bytes / step time.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import MarkdownStr, check, fmt, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_count, fmt_memory, fmt_time

class TextImageBandwidth:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    n_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Production_2K.total_accelerators  # the chapter's 2,048-GPU running cluster
    text_tokens_per_gpu = 4096  # scenario assumption: packed tokens per GPU per step
    token_bytes = BYTES_INT32
    image_batch_per_gpu = 256  # scenario assumption: images per GPU per step
    image_bytes = Datasets.ImageNet.mean_compressed_image_size  # archive size / training examples
    step = ReferenceStats.StorageTrainingCorpus.StepTime

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────
    text_bw = n_gpus * text_tokens_per_gpu * token_bytes / step
    image_bw = n_gpus * image_batch_per_gpu * image_bytes / step
    text_bw_mb_s_val = text_bw.to(MB / second).magnitude
    image_bw_gb_s_val = image_bw.to(GB / second).magnitude
    ratio_val = (image_bw / text_bw).to("").magnitude
    ratio_rounded_val = round(ratio_val / 100) * 100

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────
    check(167 < text_bw_mb_s_val < 168, "Text bandwidth should be about 168 MB/s")
    check(250 < image_bw_gb_s_val < 350, "Image bandwidth should be about 303 GB/s at the registry mean image size")
    check(1500 < ratio_val < 2100, "Image/text bandwidth ratio should be about 1,800x")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ───────────────────────────────────────
    text_bw_mb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(text_bw, unit=MB / second, precision=1, commas=False)
    image_bw_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(image_bw, unit=GB / second, precision=1, commas=False)
    ratio_rounded_mult_str = fmt_multiple(ratio_rounded_val, precision=0, commas=True)
    image_size_kb_str = fmt_qty_int(image_bytes, KB, commas=False)
    n_gpus_str = fmt(n_gpus, precision=0, commas=True)
    _n_gpus_tex = fmt(n_gpus, precision=0, commas=True).replace(",", "{,}")
    _tokens_tex = fmt(text_tokens_per_gpu, precision=0, commas=True).replace(",", "{,}")
    _token_bytes_tex = fmt_int(token_bytes.to(byte).magnitude)
    _image_kb_tex = fmt(image_bytes.to(KB).magnitude, precision=1, commas=False)
    _step_s_tex = fmt(step.to(second).magnitude, precision=1, commas=False)
    text_tokens_per_gpu_str = fmt_count(text_tokens_per_gpu, label="token")
    step_ms_str = fmt_time(step, ms, precision=0, commas=False)
    image_batch_per_gpu_str = fmt(image_batch_per_gpu, precision=0, commas=False)
    text_bw_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        f"{_n_gpus_tex} \\text{{ GPUs}} \\times {_tokens_tex} \\text{{ tokens/GPU}} "
        f"\\times {_token_bytes_tex} \\text{{ bytes/token}} \\div {_step_s_tex}\\text{{s}} "
        f"\\approx {{{text_bw_mb_per_s_str}}}"
    )
    image_bw_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        f"{_n_gpus_tex} \\text{{ GPUs}} \\times {image_batch_per_gpu} \\text{{ images/GPU}} "
        f"\\times {_image_kb_tex} \\text{{ KB/image}} \\div {_step_s_tex}\\text{{s}} "
        f"\\approx {{{image_bw_gb_per_s_str}}}"
    )
```

![](images/svg/vol2_data_storage_margin_001.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two-bar log-scale ladder: a long violet bar for image training at 303 GB/s above a short bar for text training at 168 MB/s."}

*Image training demands `{python} TextImageBandwidth.ratio_rounded_mult_str` the storage bandwidth of text.*
