:::

This abstract architecture has concrete implications for performance tuning. When a training job creates a new dataset directory on Lustre, the administrator configures the stripe count\index{Striping!stripe count} (the number of object storage targets, or OSTs, a file is spread across) and stripe size\index{Striping!stripe size} (the chunk size written to each OST) for that directory [@lustreSetstripe]. For large sequential-read training shards, administrators may choose wider striping and multi-megabyte stripe sizes so a single file can draw bandwidth from multiple OSS nodes; Lustre's striping guide treats wide striping as useful for very large files or files accessed by many clients, while smaller files often use fewer stripes to reduce overhead [@lustreFileStripingGuide]. A 4 GB data shard striped across 100 OSTs with 4 MB stripes places roughly 10 stripes on each OST. When a data loader reads large contiguous ranges, the Lustre client can issue parallel read requests to the OSS nodes holding those stripes, aggregating their bandwidth. The client also maintains its own read-ahead buffer, prefetching the next several stripes while the application processes the current ones. This file-system-level read-ahead is distinct from the data loader's application-level prefetch buffer; the two layers of prefetching compound to provide deep latency hiding, making the physical distance to the OSS nodes nearly transparent to the training process.

[^fn-oss-pfs-disambiguation]: **OSS (Object Storage Server)**\index{Object Storage Server!PFS disambiguation}: In parallel file system terminology, "object" means a chunk of striped file data managed by an object storage target, a usage that predates cloud object storage (S3, GCS) by over a decade. Confusing the two is a common source of miscommunication: when a Lustre administrator says "add more OSS nodes," they mean adding data-serving capacity to the parallel file system, not provisioning cloud buckets.

[^fn-lustre-parallel-origin]: **Lustre**\index{Lustre!etymology}: A portmanteau of "Linux" and "cluster," developed at Carnegie Mellon University and first deployed in production in 2003. Lustre is common in HPC and ML infrastructure because its architecture scales aggregate bandwidth linearly with the number of OSS nodes, the same property that makes it a natural choice for training clusters where a single job may demand hundreds of GB/s of sustained read throughput.

The separation between metadata and data paths is what enables the aggregate bandwidth that ML workloads demand. In GPFS[^fn-gpfs-parallel-filesystem] (IBM Spectrum Scale), the architecture takes a different approach: it stripes data and metadata across shared disks and coordinates concurrent access through token-based distributed locking [@schmuck2002gpfs]. The result is not a simple MDS/OSS split; it is a shared-disk design whose metadata and data placement can be distributed while the lock protocol preserves consistency across clients. The trade-off is greater complexity in lock management, which must scale to thousands of nodes.

[^fn-gpfs-parallel-filesystem]: **GPFS (General Parallel File System)**\index{GPFS!distributed metadata}: Developed by IBM Research starting in 1998, now marketed as IBM Spectrum Scale. Unlike Lustre's dedicated metadata-server/object-server organization, GPFS is a shared-disk parallel file system that can stripe data and metadata and uses token-based locking to coordinate concurrent client access. For ML checkpoint writes, this distributed coordination model can reduce reliance on a single dedicated metadata path, but it also makes lock behavior part of the performance envelope.

The data path scales with the number of object storage servers, but every file still begins with a request to the metadata service, and that service has a finite operation rate. That finite rate is the source of the small file problem\index{Small File Problem!metadata bottleneck}. The per-open cost that @sec-storage-data-formats charged to one node's CPU now lands on a metadata service shared by the whole fleet. Each `open()` system call requires a metadata lookup, lock acquisition, and attribute fetch. When a dataset of millions of 10 KB images is stored as individual files and 10,000 workers, a fleet several times the running cluster, each open a new file every few samples, the aggregate open rate exceeds the few hundred thousand operations per second an MDS typically serves. The MDS becomes the serialization point, and delivery collapses to its operation rate long before the data links saturate.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{15\baselineskip}
```

::: {#dfn-data-storage-small-file-problem .callout-definition title="Small file problem"}

***Small file problem***\index{Small File Problem!definition} is an ML data-loading pathology in which per-file operations overwhelm a storage system's metadata service.

1.  **Significance**: `open`, `stat`, and `close` requests from 10,000 workers can serialize at the metadata service, idle the cluster, and reduce effective I/O bandwidth $(\Bandwidth_{\text{IO}})$.
2.  **Distinction**: This is a metadata request-rate and latency $(\Latency)$ problem, not a bulk bit-rate problem.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Faster SSDs do not fix this format problem\index{Small File Problem!format packaging}. Packing samples into sequential containers such as TFRecord\index{TFRecord!sequential container} or Parquet amortizes metadata operations across many samples.

:::

At production scale, the metadata bottleneck can collapse an otherwise high-bandwidth file system.

::: {#exmp-data-storage-metadata-meltdown .callout-example title="The metadata meltdown"}

**Scenario**: A large-scale training cluster migrates from a preprocessed sequential dataset to 200 million raw image files stored individually on a parallel file system provisioned for 500 GB/s aggregate bandwidth.

**Diagnosis**: The file system delivers less than 1 percent of rated throughput. Millions of per-second `stat()` and `open()` calls overwhelm the metadata servers, choking data loaders despite abundant network and storage bandwidth.

**Systems lesson**: Metadata contention limits delivery when operation demand exceeds metadata service capacity. Bundling 200 million raw images into 50,000 large tar shards (for example, WebDataset) reduces the file count by 4,000$\times$ and amortizes per-file operations across samples. Packaging alone does not prevent startup contention if loaders still enumerate files with per-file `stat()` calls; distributing a precomputed dataset manifest removes those repeated lookups from the hot path. Measure metadata operation rate alongside byte bandwidth to determine which service limits delivery.

:::

Striping\index{Striping!data distribution} and aggregation\index{Aggregation!small-file mitigation} solve different problems. Striping distributes large files across data servers; aggregation, the shard packaging of @sec-storage-data-formats, reduces the number of files the MDS must track. Realized bandwidth depends on the reader. A read contained within one stripe uses one server, while enough concurrent reads spanning stripes can use several servers. Wider striping helps only when the read sizes and concurrency exploit those paths; small files usually need fewer stripes.

Parallel file systems provide a shared namespace and lock management that support coordinated checkpoints\index{Checkpointing!shared namespace coordination} [@schmuck2002gpfs]. Recovery requires every reader of a committed checkpoint to observe the same completed state. The file system supplies storage primitives, but the training system must coordinate the shards into one restorable generation. A completed write to one file does not establish that all other checkpoint files are complete.

The consistency model has subtleties that matter for ML workloads. For training data reads, immutable shards remove conflicts with concurrent writers once the dataset version has been published. Readers must still agree on which completed version belongs to the run. Checkpoints require more. File-system locks can coordinate individual writes, but they do not by themselves make a checkpoint that spans many files atomic, so a multi-file generation needs an application-level publication protocol, developed in @sec-storage-checkpointing.

The performance of a parallel file system depends not only on the *number* of OSS nodes but also on the *balance* of load across them. If a shard uses 10 of 100 equally provisioned OSS nodes, those servers offer at most 10 percent of the system's aggregate server bandwidth. Realized delivery can be lower because of client limits, request size, or insufficient concurrency. Conversely, when many concurrent readers draw on shards striped across all 100 servers, demand spreads over every server and realized bandwidth can approach the system's rating, provided the clients and network keep pace. Placement and access scheduling therefore matter alongside the number of storage servers.

At the scale of thousands of nodes, tail latency [@dean2013] can dominate exposed input wait. If a training step requires data from 100 storage servers and each independently has a 1 percent chance of being slow, the probability that all 100 respond quickly is $0.99^{100} = 0.366$, meaning over 63 percent of these request sets contain at least one slow response. Shared congestion can correlate delays, changing that probability. A slow response delays the step only when prefetching fails to hide it and the required input lies on the step's critical path. When it does, the delay is not confined to one worker, because synchronous data-parallel training waits for every worker at the next collective, so one late fetch stretches the whole fleet's step.

Systems can mitigate tail latency through hedged requests\index{Hedged requests!tail latency mitigation}: after a chosen delay, the client issues a redundant read to another replica and uses the first valid response. The trigger delay trades faster tail completion against extra work [@dean2013tail]. An independence model can multiply the probabilities of two slow replicas, but shared congestion and the later start of the hedge invalidate a simple squared-probability latency guarantee. Issuing a hedge at the median response time would duplicate roughly half of requests before accounting for cancellation; that load can worsen the congestion the scheme aims to avoid. A hedge therefore pays off only when its trigger sits in the measured tail and the duplicate traffic it adds stays within the spare service capacity.

The effectiveness of hedged requests depends on the replicated data layout. If both replicas reside on OSS nodes that share the same network switch, a switch failure makes both copies simultaneously unavailable. Effective hedging requires failure-domain-aware placement\index{Failure-domain-aware placement!replica distribution}: replicas should reside in different racks, connected through different top-of-rack switches, so that the failure of any single component affects at most one replica.

In production clusters, the parallel file system is a shared utility, simultaneously servicing dozens of concurrent training jobs with different I/O patterns. At any given moment, a large language model job might be streaming sequentially through text shards, a computer vision job might be reading random image shards, and a checkpoint storm from a third job could be saturating write bandwidth. This concurrency gives rise to the noisy neighbor problem\index{Noisy neighbor problem!PFS interference}, where one job's I/O pattern severely degrades performance for all other jobs. A checkpoint save that consumes a disproportionate share of the PFS's internal network bandwidth causes read latency for other jobs to spike, potentially stalling their training pipelines. PFS administrators mitigate this through I/O scheduling policies (quality-of-service tiers, bandwidth quotas per job), but these policies add administrative complexity and can reduce peak single-job throughput.

A related challenge is namespace isolation\index{Namespace isolation!striping configuration}. Different teams and workloads require different storage configurations. A team training on millions of 100 KB images first needs to aggregate samples to reduce metadata operations; increasing stripe count does not remove per-file metadata work. A team working with large video shards can use wider striping when read sizes and concurrency exploit the additional data paths. Misconfigured striping for one team's workload can create hotspots that degrade performance for the entire shared file system. The impact of sharing is easy to quantify: a PFS with 1 TB/s aggregate bandwidth, shared across 10 concurrent training jobs, provides only 100 GB/s per job on average. If one job's checkpoint storm consumes 400 GB/s for 10 seconds, the remaining nine jobs share 600 GB/s, a 33 percent reduction that can trigger data stalls in their accelerator pipelines.

::: {#chk-data-storage-parallel-file-system-design .callout-checkpoint title="Parallel file system design"}

Consider a training cluster with 512 nodes, each running 8 GPUs. The training job requires 400 GB/s of aggregate read bandwidth.

- [ ] **OSS count**: calculate the number of OSS nodes required when each Lustre OSS delivers 10 GB/s.
- [ ] **Metadata cost**: calculate the time required to open 200 million `{python} TextImageBandwidth.image_size_kb_str` image files sequentially when each `open()` call takes 50 $\mu$s on the MDS, then state the practical implication.
- [ ] **Shard count**: calculate the number of metadata operations needed to read the full dataset when images are bundled into 4 GB tar files.

:::

Parallel file systems solve the shared-namespace problem for active training clusters, but their cost per byte is too high for the organization's complete data holdings. The petabytes of raw training data, historical checkpoints, and preprocessed datasets that an ML organization accumulates over years require a tier optimized for capacity and durability rather than bandwidth.

### Tier 4 object storage {#sec-storage-tier4-object}

At the scale of petabytes, object storage\index{Object Storage!cloud storage tier} provides the durable, cost-effective foundation of the hierarchy. Services like Amazon S3\index{Amazon S3!key-value namespace} and Google Cloud Storage\index{Google Cloud Storage!key-value namespace} organize data in object namespaces where objects are retrieved by keys rather than by POSIX directory paths [@awsS3ObjectKeys; @googleCloudStorageObjects]. Unlike file systems, which organize data in hierarchical directories with metadata-rich operations (rename, link, permission inheritance), object storage treats each object as an opaque blob identified by a unique key. The simpler interface changes the namespace operations exposed to clients; the service still manages metadata for placement, versions, access control, and integrity as capacity grows.

Services such as Amazon S3 publish an "eleven nines"[^fn-durability-nines-availability] annual durability target (99.999999999 percent). Erasure coding,[^fn-reedsolomon-erasure-coding] replication, placement, and repair contribute to storage protection, but a coding scheme alone does not establish a service's durability target. Selecting a source-of-truth tier for training data and checkpoint archives requires checking the chosen service's failure model alongside versioning, lifecycle policy, access control, and recovery testing.

Three different guarantees govern whether that source of truth is usable. Durability\index{Durability!storage} asks whether acknowledged data survives failures; availability\index{Availability!storage} asks whether the storage service responds when a client needs it; and consistency\index{Consistency!storage} asks which version a read is allowed to observe when writes overlap or replicas disagree. Replication can improve durability and availability without by itself guaranteeing that a reader sees the newest committed checkpoint. A recovery design must therefore state all three properties instead of treating a durability percentage as a complete reliability contract.

[^fn-reedsolomon-erasure-coding]: **Erasure Coding**\index{Erasure Coding!Reed-Solomon codes}: Built on Reed-Solomon codes [@reed1960], which use maximum-distance-separable coding to recover the original data from any sufficient subset of encoded fragments. In storage systems, Reed-Solomon-style codes and later local-reconstruction variants trade storage overhead against repair bandwidth and degraded-read cost [@plank1997; @huang2012erasure]. Local-reconstruction codes, for example, read fewer surviving fragments to rebuild a lost one, cutting repair traffic at the price of a little extra capacity.

[^fn-durability-nines-availability]: **Eleven Nines (99.999999999 Percent Durability)**\index{Durability!eleven nines}: A design target of 11 nines annual durability corresponds to an expected loss probability of about $10^{-11}$ per object-year; for one million objects, that is about one expected object loss per 100,000 years. The same service indirection, erasure coding, replication, and metadata lookup that support durability also make object storage a higher-latency tier than local NVMe or a warm parallel file system, so real-time data pipelines need prefetch buffering.

::: {#dfn-data-storage-erasure-coding .callout-definition title="Erasure coding"}

***Erasure coding***\index{Erasure Coding!definition} protects stored data by adding redundant fragments, with the Reed-Solomon scheme considered here encoding $k$ data and $m$ parity blocks so that any $k$ remaining fragments recover the original.

1.  **Significance**: Coding can protect against fragment loss with less capacity overhead than full replication. A 4+2 Reed-Solomon code stores four data fragments and two parity fragments, tolerating two unavailable fragments at 1.5$\times$ storage overhead instead of the 3$\times$ overhead of triple replication. Actual durability also depends on failure correlation, placement, detection, and repair.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike replication (which stores complete copies), erasure coding uses mathematical encoding (for example, Reed-Solomon) to distribute redundant information across different failure domains (disks, racks, or sites).
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that erasure coding is "free durability." In reality, it is a latency-compute trade-off\index{Latency!compute trade-off}: reconstructing data after a failure requires additional CPU cycles and increases the p99 latency of the storage read.

:::

Erasure coding lets the service recover data without requiring the training application to manage fragments. In the form considered here, the service retains the original $k$ data fragments alongside parity, so healthy reads can use the data fragments directly. When a required fragment is unavailable, reconstruction uses surviving data and parity fragments. The object interface hides that recovery procedure, but additional I/O, network traffic, and decoding can remain visible as longer read latency. Protection against data loss does not imply unchanged service time during a failure.

```{python}
#| echo: false

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ OBJECT STORAGE ANNUAL COST COMPARISON
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Tier 4 rate ratio and @sec-storage-economics 100 TB tier costs;
# │          the single computation of the 100 TB S3, NVMe, and egress costs.
# │
# │ Goal:    Quantify yearly storage cost at the object and NVMe tiers.
# │ Show:    $24,000/yr for S3 Standard (low tier); $120,000/yr for NVMe.
# │ How:     100 TB × 1000 GB/TB × $/GB/month × 12 months.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

class ObjectStorageCost:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    dataset_size_tb = 100
    cost_s3_gb_mo = Infrastructure.Pricing.Storage.S3StandardLowPerTbMonth.rate.to(USD / (GB * ureg.month)).magnitude
    cost_nvme_gb_mo = Infrastructure.Pricing.Storage.NvmeLowPerTbMonth.rate.to(USD / (GB * ureg.month)).magnitude

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────
    s3_annual_val = dataset_size_tb * THOUSAND * cost_s3_gb_mo * 12
    nvme_annual_val = dataset_size_tb * THOUSAND * cost_nvme_gb_mo * 12

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────
    from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_usd

    check(nvme_annual_val > s3_annual_val, "NVMe cost should be higher than S3")
    nvme_s3_ratio_val = cost_nvme_gb_mo / cost_s3_gb_mo
    egress_rate = Infrastructure.Pricing.Cloud.EgressPerGB.rate
    egress_once_val = (dataset_size_tb * TB * egress_rate).to(USD).magnitude

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ───────────────────────────────────────
    s3_annual_usd_str = fmt_usd(s3_annual_val, precision=0)
    nvme_annual_usd_str = fmt_usd(nvme_annual_val, precision=0)
    s3_rate_gb_mo_str = fmt_usd(cost_s3_gb_mo, precision=2, commas=False, per="GB/month")
    nvme_s3_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(nvme_s3_ratio_val, precision=0, commas=False)
    dataset_tb_str = fmt_memory(dataset_size_tb * TB, unit=TB, precision=0, commas=False)
    egress_once_usd_str = fmt_usd(egress_once_val, precision=0)
```

The cost advantage of object storage is significant: at a representative `{python} ObjectStorageCost.s3_rate_gb_mo_str`, its recurring capacity rate is `{python} ObjectStorageCost.nvme_s3_ratio_mult_str` lower than the local-NVMe rate assumed here, and @sec-storage-economics converts that ratio into annual costs for a `{python} ObjectStorageCost.dataset_tb_str` dataset. Comparing it with HBM acquisition cost additionally requires a hardware lifetime and utilization assumption. This cost advantage makes object storage a common home for the organization's training data lake, where raw data, preprocessed datasets, and archived model artifacts can reside durably.

Request latency also matters. Design estimates use 50 to 100 ms for an object GET as a representative planning range rather than a universal service guarantee. Much of that delay is the price of the indirection that provides durability. The service looks up the object's location in a distributed metadata index, determines which fragments to read, fetches them from potentially different storage nodes, and reconstructs data when a fragment is unavailable, all on top of the client network path and queueing. Large transfers amortize per-request overhead across more bytes, while small transfers can spend most of their elapsed time on that overhead. Request size and concurrency therefore enter the delivery budget alongside aggregate bandwidth.

The remedy is the shard packaging of @sec-storage-data-formats, applied here to request latency rather than metadata operations. Formats like WebDataset\index{WebDataset!object storage streaming} [@aizman2019] or Mosaic Streaming\index{Mosaic Streaming!object storage streaming} [@mosaicStreamingMainConcepts] bundle samples into multi-gigabyte shards that transform high-latency random access into high-bandwidth sequential streaming. Rather than issuing billions of small GET requests, the data loader issues hundreds of large reads in parallel, each fetching an entire shard that contains thousands of samples. With sufficient parallelism and colocated network capacity, object storage can sustain high aggregate throughput, enough to feed large training clusters for some workloads. The streaming pattern works by assigning each data loader worker a subset of shards and having it read them sequentially. Within each shard, samples are stored contiguously, so the worker decodes them in order and shuffles them in a local buffer. This approach achieves pseudo-random access across the dataset while maintaining sequential I/O at the storage level.

The architecture of a streaming data loader\index{Data loader!object storage streaming} for object storage differs from a local-storage loader in important ways. A local-storage loader can use memory-mapped I/O to treat the dataset as a virtual memory region, relying on the operating system's page fault mechanism to load data on demand. This approach is elegant but incompatible with object storage, which does not support the POSIX file system interface that memory mapping requires. Instead, an object-storage loader must explicitly manage HTTP connections, issue ranged GET requests for specific byte ranges within shards, handle retries on transient failures, and manage a local buffer pool for decoded samples. Libraries like WebDataset and Mosaic Streaming encapsulate this complexity, presenting a simple iterator interface to the training loop while managing the HTTP transport and buffering internally.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: object-storage streaming paragraph
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_memory

class ObjectStreamContext:
    training_tokens = ReferenceStats.StorageTrainingCorpus.TrainingTokens
    token_id_bytes = ReferenceStats.StorageTrainingCorpus.TokenIdBytes
    tokenized_shard = ReferenceStats.StorageTrainingCorpus.TokenizedShardSize
    step = ReferenceStats.StorageTrainingCorpus.StepTime
    n_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Production_2K.total_accelerators  # the chapter's 2,048-GPU running cluster
    tokens_per_gpu = 4096  # scenario assumption: packed tokens per GPU per step
    tokenized_text = training_tokens * token_id_bytes
    tokenized_shard_count_val = round((tokenized_text / tokenized_shard).to("").magnitude)
    text_bw = n_gpus * tokens_per_gpu * token_id_bytes / step
    n_nodes = Systems.Clusters.Production_2K.count  # the chapter's 256-node running cluster
    workers_per_node = 8  # scenario assumption: data-loader workers per node
    shards_per_node_val = round(tokenized_shard_count_val / n_nodes)
    concurrent_requests_val = n_nodes * workers_per_node
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    text_bw_mb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(text_bw, unit=MB / second, precision=1, commas=False)
    tokenized_shard_count_str = fmt(tokenized_shard_count_val, precision=0)
    tokenized_shard_gb_str = fmt_memory(tokenized_shard, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    n_nodes_str = fmt_count(n_nodes, commas=True)
    workers_per_node_str = fmt_int(workers_per_node)
    shards_per_node_str = fmt_int(shards_per_node_val)
    concurrent_requests_str = fmt_count(concurrent_requests_val, commas=True)
```
Applying this streaming architecture to the running example makes the design concrete as an alternative to the staged path the chapter adopts. Instead of copying shards to local NVMe at job start, the cluster would read them from the object store throughout the run. The tokenized training set is stored in an S3-like object store as roughly `{python} ObjectStreamContext.tokenized_shard_count_str` shards of `{python} ObjectStreamContext.tokenized_shard_gb_str` each. The streaming architecture assigns each of the `{python} ObjectStreamContext.n_nodes_str` compute nodes a unique subset of roughly `{python} ObjectStreamContext.shards_per_node_str` shards. Within each node, `{python} ObjectStreamContext.workers_per_node_str` data loader worker processes issue concurrent HTTP `Range` requests to fetch 256 MB chunks from their assigned shards. Across the cluster, this results in `{python} ObjectStreamContext.concurrent_requests_str` concurrent requests, allowing aggregate throughput in the 50--100 GB/s range when the object store and network path are provisioned for it, far exceeding the roughly `{python} ObjectStreamContext.text_bw_mb_per_s_str` required for text model training. In this regime, the bottleneck often shifts from the object store's bandwidth to the network bandwidth between the compute virtual private cloud (VPC) and the object-storage endpoint. Organizations that co-locate compute and storage in the same cloud availability zone can reduce cross-network latency, directly reducing the required prefetch buffer depth and improving overall pipeline efficiency.

That request parallelism is what object storage rewards. Each of the `{python} ObjectStreamContext.concurrent_requests_str` GET requests is independent and can be served by a different storage node within the cloud provider's infrastructure, and the count grows with the fleet. With each request fetching a 256 MB chunk of a shard, the aggregate throughput depends on the cloud provider's network capacity, internal bandwidth, and request-rate quotas. The practical limit is often the network bandwidth between the compute cluster and the object storage service, not the storage service's internal media bandwidth.

Many object storage services provide strong read-after-write consistency\index{Consistency!read-after-write}, which means that a subsequent read of an acknowledged object sees the completed write. Amazon S3 announced strong read-after-write consistency for object writes and overwrites, together with strongly consistent listing, in December 2020 [@aws2020s3]. The relevant contract is the documented behavior of the chosen backend, not a blanket assumption about object storage. Per-object consistency still does not make a checkpoint spanning many objects atomic, so the publication protocol of @sec-storage-checkpointing applies here as it does on a file system.

The immense scale of ML datasets makes them vulnerable to silent data corruption\index{Silent Data Corruption!bit flips and degradation}: subtle bit flips in the storage medium or during network transfer that can introduce training artifacts nearly impossible to diagnose. Object storage services provide per-object checksums\index{Checksum!object storage verification} that verify integrity on upload, copy, or download; Amazon S3, for example, documents checksum options including CRC-family and cryptographic hashes [@awsS3ObjectIntegrity]. Parallel file systems often rely on underlying RAID or erasure coding for physical integrity but may not provide end-to-end checksums visible to the application. A robust large-scale ML pipeline computes and stores a checksum for each data shard during preprocessing and verifies it when the shard is first loaded by a training worker. The verification overhead is negligible compared to the cost of training on corrupted data. For model checkpoints, integrity verification is even more critical: a single bit flip in a weight or optimizer state can corrupt the model, causing training to diverge silently after recovery. Frameworks and checkpoint libraries can include integrity verification, but the pipeline should not assume it without testing the checkpoint format.

Training datasets can contain sensitive information, including personal data, proprietary text, and licensed images. Storage design must carry the organization's access and retention policies through every copy. Object services expose identity policies and encryption options; parallel file systems provide POSIX permissions\index{POSIX!permissions and ACLs} and access-control lists. Audit coverage and enforcement depend on the configured platform, not the tier's name. Versioned manifests should identify derived shards and retained copies so that access reviews, retention decisions, and deletion workflows can locate the relevant artifacts; a deletion request, for example, must reach every immutable preprocessed shard derived from the deleted record. Storage controls protect stored bytes; evaluating what a trained model retains requires additional model-level analysis.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: storage-glacier-cost-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ARCHIVE TIER ANNUAL COST
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-storage-tier5-archive rate ratio and the 100 TB archive cost
# │          quoted in @sec-storage-economics.
# │
# │ Goal:    Compute annual Glacier cost for 100 TB dataset.
# │ Show:    $4,800/year at $0.004/GB/month.
# │ How:     100 TB × 1000 GB/TB × $0.004/GB/month × 12 months.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Infrastructure, GB, THOUSAND, USD, ureg
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_usd

class GlacierCost:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    dataset_size_tb = 100
    cost_glacier_gb_mo = Infrastructure.Pricing.Storage.GlacierStandardPerTbMonth.rate.to(USD / (GB * ureg.month)).magnitude

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────
    dataset_size = dataset_size_tb * THOUSAND * GB
    glacier_annual_cost = dataset_size * (cost_glacier_gb_mo * USD / (GB * ureg.month)) * 12 * ureg.month

    cost_s3_gb_mo = Infrastructure.Pricing.Storage.S3StandardLowPerTbMonth.rate.to(USD / (GB * ureg.month)).magnitude
    s3_glacier_ratio_val = cost_s3_gb_mo / cost_glacier_gb_mo

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────
    check(glacier_annual_cost.to(USD).magnitude > 0, "Glacier annual cost should be positive")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ───────────────────────────────────────
    glacier_annual_usd_str = fmt_usd(glacier_annual_cost, precision=0)
    glacier_rate_gb_mo_str = fmt_usd(cost_glacier_gb_mo, precision=3, commas=False, per="GB/month")
    s3_rate_gb_mo_str = fmt_usd(cost_s3_gb_mo, precision=2, commas=False, per="GB/month")
    s3_glacier_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(s3_glacier_ratio_val, precision=0, commas=False)
    dataset_tb_str = fmt_memory(dataset_size, unit=TB, precision=0, commas=False)
```

The transition from Tier 4 to Tier 5 is driven primarily by economics. Data that is accessed rarely should move to archive storage when retrieval latency and governance requirements allow it, because archive capacity is cheaper still.

### Tier 5 archive and cold storage {#sec-storage-tier5-archive}

The final tier provides long-term preservation for compliance and auditability. Archive services (such as S3 Glacier) are designed for data that is rarely accessed: training logs from previous years, superseded model checkpoints, audit trails for regulatory compliance. At a representative `{python} GlacierCost.glacier_rate_gb_mo_str`, archive storage is `{python} GlacierCost.s3_glacier_ratio_mult_str` cheaper than the `{python} GlacierCost.s3_rate_gb_mo_str` object-storage assumption used in @sec-storage-tier4-object. The trade-off is retrieval latency measured in minutes to hours, making this tier unsuitable for operational access.

The primary value of archive storage is organizational memory. When a model trained two years ago produces unexpected behavior in production, the ability to recover the exact training data, hyperparameters, and intermediate checkpoints for forensic analysis depends on archive storage. Organizations that aggressively purge old data to save costs discover, often at the worst possible moment, that they cannot reproduce or explain the behavior of deployed models.

Automated lifecycle policies\index{Lifecycle policy!storage tier transitions} govern the transition of data between tiers based on access recency. As one illustration of how such automation is expressed, a time-based rule for ML infrastructure might move checkpoints as follows: the most recent three checkpoints remain on the parallel file system for fast recovery; checkpoints older than 72 hours are transitioned to object storage; checkpoints older than 90 days are transitioned to archive storage; and checkpoints older than two years are deleted unless flagged for regulatory retention. S3 Lifecycle rules provide the same general transition/archive/delete mechanism for object lifetimes [@awsS3LifecycleManagement]. The running example's checkpoint retention in @sec-storage-checkpointing adopts a count-based variant of the same idea, where the transition rule keys on checkpoint count rather than age. Without automation, teams either hoard data on expensive tiers (wasting budget) or delete data too aggressively (losing reproducibility). The lifecycle policy encodes the organization's cost-recovery trade-off in a declarative rule that requires no manual intervention.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-storage-tier5-archive
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_count, fmt_memory, fmt_ratio

class ArchiveLineageContext:
    training_tokens = ReferenceStats.StorageTrainingCorpus.TrainingTokens
    compressed_text = ReferenceStats.StorageTrainingCorpus.CompressedSource
    token_id_bytes = ReferenceStats.StorageTrainingCorpus.TokenIdBytes
    tokenized_text = training_tokens * token_id_bytes
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    compressed_text_tb_str = fmt_memory(compressed_text, unit=TB, precision=0, commas=False)
    tokenized_text_tb_str = fmt_memory(tokenized_text, unit=TB, precision=0, commas=False)
```
For the 175B model training run, the archive tier holds the complete training lineage: the raw `{python} ArchiveLineageContext.compressed_text_tb_str` compressed source corpus, the `{python} ArchiveLineageContext.tokenized_text_tb_str` serialized shard set, all preprocessing scripts, the final checkpoint, and a sampled subset of intermediate checkpoints. Capacity must include every retained full checkpoint as well as both corpus representations; @tbl-data-storage-175b-footprint computes that total for the declared retention policy. A round dataset-only allowance would underprovision the archive. The asymmetry between archive cost and compute cost makes retention inexpensive relative to the run it documents; failures to archive usually reflect missing lifecycle ownership, unclear retention policy, or retrieval-process neglect rather than raw capacity cost.

Archive storage services offer multiple retrieval speed tiers, each with different pricing. In an S3 Glacier-style service, standard retrieval may complete within hours at moderate cost, expedited retrieval may complete within minutes at a higher cost, and bulk retrieval may trade still more latency for the lowest retrieval price [@awsS3GlacierRetrieval]. The choice of retrieval tier depends on the urgency of the use case. Forensic analysis of a production incident warrants faster retrieval; annual compliance audits can use slower bulk retrieval. Designing the lifecycle policy\index{Lifecycle policy!storage tiering} requires understanding the storage cost, the expected retrieval frequency, and the urgency for each class of data.

Training data provenance\index{Data provenance!regulatory compliance} links a deployed model to the data versions and preprocessing that produced it. The organization's governance policy determines which records to retain and for how long; the storage design must make those records identifiable and retrievable throughout that period. Archive is a candidate when its retrieval delay meets that requirement. Records needed during frequent investigations may justify a warmer tier even when archival capacity is cheaper.

The six tiers now have their roles, capacities, and prices, but a role does not say how fast bytes must climb the hierarchy. That rate is set by the accelerators consuming them, and it is the next quantity to derive.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: storage-pipeline-equation-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ DATA PIPELINE BANDWIDTH AND STALL CALCULATIONS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-storage-pipeline-equation—required aggregate bandwidth for
# │          ImageNet-scale training and data stall ratio with pipelining.
# │
# │ Goal:    Derive the required storage bandwidth for 256-GPU ImageNet training
# │          and show the 20% stall from a 250 ms I/O vs 200 ms compute overlap.
# │ Show:    ~30.3 GB/s required; 20% stall; rendered display equation.
# │ How:     BW = N_gpu × U × (batch × img_size) / T_step; stall = (max-comp)/max.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import MarkdownStr, check, fmt, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_time
import math

class PipelineCalcs:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    n_gpus_image = 256  # scenario assumption: separate image-training job size
    img_size = Datasets.ImageNet.mean_compressed_image_size  # archive size / training examples
    batch_img_gpu = 256  # scenario assumption: images per GPU per step
    util_target = 0.80  # scenario assumption: target active-time fraction
    t_step = ReferenceStats.StorageTrainingCorpus.StepTime
    t_comp = ReferenceStats.StorageTrainingCorpus.StepTime
    t_io = 250 * ms  # scenario assumption: I/O time per batch

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────
    req_bw_imagenet = n_gpus_image * util_target * batch_img_gpu * img_size / t_step
    req_bw_imagenet_gbs_val = req_bw_imagenet.to(GB / second).magnitude
    stall_max_t = max(t_comp, t_io)
    data_stall_pct_val = ((stall_max_t - t_comp) / stall_max_t).to("").magnitude * 100
    t_step_seq = t_io + t_comp  # no overlap: I/O then compute
    stall_seq_val = (t_io / t_step_seq).to("").magnitude * 100

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────
    check(req_bw_imagenet_gbs_val > 10, f"ImageNet aggregate BW should be high, got {req_bw_imagenet_gbs_val:.1f} GB/s")
    check(data_stall_pct_val == 20, "Data stall calculation mismatch")
    check(54 < stall_seq_val < 57, "Sequential stall should be about 55.6%")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ───────────────────────────────────────
    req_bw_imagenet_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(req_bw_imagenet, unit=GB / second, precision=1, commas=False)
    n_gpus_image_str = fmt_count(n_gpus_image, commas=False)
    t_step_ms_str = fmt_time(t_step, ms, precision=0, commas=False)
    util_target_str = fmt_percent(util_target, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    img_size_kb_str = fmt_qty_int(img_size, KB, commas=False)
    data_stall_pct_str = fmt_percent(data_stall_pct_val / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    t_comp_stall_str = fmt_time(t_comp, ms, precision=0, commas=False)
    t_io_stall_str = fmt_time(t_io, ms, precision=0, commas=False)

    _io_ms = t_io.to(ms).magnitude
    _comp_ms = t_comp.to(ms).magnitude
    _seq_ms = t_step_seq.to(ms).magnitude
    _pipe_ms = stall_max_t.to(ms).magnitude

    stall_pct_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        f"\\text{{Stall \\%}} = \\frac{{{_io_ms:.0f} - {_comp_ms:.0f}}}" f"{{{_io_ms:.0f}}} = " f"{{{data_stall_pct_val:.0f}\\%}}"
    )
    tstep_seq_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        f"T_{{\\text{{step}}}} = T_{{\\text{{IO}}}} + T_{{\\text{{compute}}}} = " f"{_io_ms:.0f} + {_comp_ms:.0f} = {_seq_ms:.0f} \\text{{ ms}}"
    )
    stall_seq_display_math = fmt_display_math(f"\\text{{Stall \\%}} = \\frac{{{_io_ms:.0f}}}{{{_seq_ms:.0f}}} = " f"{stall_seq_val:.1f}\\%")
    tstep_pipe_display_math = fmt_display_math(f"T_{{\\text{{step}}}} = \\max({_comp_ms:.0f}, {_io_ms:.0f}) = {_pipe_ms:.0f} \\text{{ ms}}")
```

## The Data Pipeline Equation {#sec-storage-pipeline-equation}

Every training job eventually raises the concrete sizing question of how much storage bandwidth the pipeline must deliver before accelerators stall. The required rate depends on the training configuration, and miscalculating in either direction is expensive. Under-provisioning storage bandwidth starves accelerators. Over-provisioning wastes budget on storage capacity that sits partially idle. The data pipeline throughput equation\index{Data pipeline!throughput equation} in @eq-pipeline-throughput quantifies the bandwidth the pipeline must sustain for a target training rate:

$$\Bandwidth_{\text{required}} = \AcceleratorCountGpu \times \eta_{\text{target}} \times \frac{D_{\text{vol,batch}}}{\IronlawTermTimesCompute}$$ {#eq-pipeline-throughput}

where $\AcceleratorCountGpu$ counts accelerators consuming distinct local input batches, $\eta_{\text{target}}$ is the target fraction of wall-clock time spent computing (typically 0.8 to 0.95), $D_{\text{vol,batch}}$ is one local batch in bytes, and $\IronlawTermTimesCompute$ is its uninterrupted compute time. This utilization is an active-time fraction, not model FLOPs utilization. If iteration time already includes stalls, multiplying by utilization again would count the slowdown twice. Eliminating sustained input stalls requires supplying batches at the full compute rate; the target fraction sizes a lower accepted training rate. Devices that cooperate on one batch do not each require an independent storage read, so their shared input must be counted once at the tier being sized. The text-versus-image comparison of notebook \ref{nbk-data-storage-text-vs-image-bandwidth} already applied this equation with $\eta_{\text{target}} = 1$; the equation makes the target fraction explicit, and the service chain below adds the requirement that every stage, not only the accelerator-facing endpoint, meet the resulting rate.

The demand equation sizes the accelerator-facing endpoint, but bytes must traverse the complete service chain. Let $r_k$ denote the measured service rate of stage $k$, including object-store reads, network transfer, decoding and augmentation, host-memory copies, and host-to-device transfer. Express all rates in the same output-equivalent bytes per second, using each stage's expansion or compression ratio; raw compressed-read bandwidth cannot be compared directly with decoded-tensor bandwidth. With bounded buffers and no sustained backlog, the pipeline can deliver at most

$$r_{\text{pipeline}} = \min_k r_k, \qquad r_{\text{pipeline}} \geq \Bandwidth_{\text{required}}.$$ {#eq-storage-service-chain}

Capacity at one tier cannot compensate for a slower downstream stage. Compression may raise the storage-read rate while lowering the decode rate; additional loader workers may raise decoding throughput while saturating the host-memory or PCIe stage. The end-to-end inequality in @eq-storage-service-chain therefore turns the chapter's hierarchy into a testable contract: measure every stage under representative concurrency, then provision or overlap the stage whose service rate is the minimum.

The throughput equation in @eq-pipeline-throughput exposes four levers on storage demand, and none of them is free. Reducing the accelerator count ($\AcceleratorCountGpu$) lowers aggregate input demand by reducing the number of distinct consumers, but it lowers training throughput with it. Lowering target utilization ($\eta_{\text{target}}$) relaxes the delivery rate by accepting idle accelerators. Decreasing the per-batch data volume ($D_{\text{vol,batch}}$) through a more compact representation of the same samples helps only while decoding keeps pace; shrinking the batch itself changes the training configuration and its statistical efficiency. Increasing compute time ($\IronlawTermTimesCompute$) gives storage longer to deliver each batch, but every iteration takes proportionally longer, which is also why a faster accelerator can expose an input bottleneck the slower one hid. The equation therefore sizes the pipeline for a chosen training configuration; deliberately slowing useful computation does not improve delivery.

As a separate image-training example, consider `{python} PipelineCalcs.n_gpus_image_str` GPUs training with ImageNet-scale images, `{python} PipelineCalcs.t_step_ms_str` iterations, and `{python} PipelineCalcs.util_target_str` target utilization. This configuration requires `{python} PipelineCalcs.req_bw_imagenet_gb_per_s_str` of aggregate storage throughput. The bandwidth must be sustained continuously for the duration of training, which may last days or weeks. If sustained delivery falls below `{python} PipelineCalcs.req_bw_imagenet_gb_per_s_str`, the input path cannot support that target rate once its buffers drain. For the chapter's 175B language-model running example, tokenized text has a much lower per-batch bandwidth demand, but the total data volume and checkpoint traffic over the run are much larger, shifting the bottleneck from peak training-data bandwidth to sustained throughput and checkpoint movement over weeks.

The consequences of falling short are captured by the **data stall ratio**\index{Data Stall Ratio!definition}, defined in @eq-data-stall as the fraction of each training step where the accelerator waits for data:

$$\text{Data Stall \%} = \frac{T_{\text{step}} - \IronlawTermTimesCompute}{T_{\text{step}}} \times 100$$ {#eq-data-stall}

@Eq-data-stall describes one worker's input path with communication excluded, so its $T_{\text{step}}$ is compute plus exposed input wait. The Fleet Law of @sec-vol2-introduction-fleet-law carries no input-wait term, so it implicitly treats the next batch as already resident; whatever input wait the loader fails to hide adds to the distributed step on top of $\CommunicationTime$ and $\SynchronizationTime$, as compute ($C_1$) capacity that sits idle while storage catches up. In a real distributed job, the gap $T_{\text{step}} - \IronlawTermTimesCompute$ also contains exposed communication and synchronization, so the ratio implicates storage only when that gap is measured as time spent waiting on the input queue, separately from collectives and barriers. Without overlap, step time adds compute and I/O time. Pipelining reduces step time to the longer of the two durations and stall time to the positive difference between I/O and compute.

::: {#nbk-data-storage-data-stall-ratio .callout-notebook title="The data stall ratio"}

**Problem**: A GPU processes a batch in `{python} PipelineCalcs.t_comp_stall_str`, but storage takes `{python} PipelineCalcs.t_io_stall_str` to deliver the next batch. What fraction of each training step is the accelerator idle, and how much does pipelining I/O with compute reduce that stall?

*Without pipelining* (sequential I/O then compute):

`{python} PipelineCalcs.tstep_seq_display_math`
`{python} PipelineCalcs.stall_seq_display_math`

*With pipelining* (I/O overlapped with compute):

`{python} PipelineCalcs.tstep_pipe_display_math`
`{python} PipelineCalcs.stall_pct_display_math`

**Systems insight**: Even with pipelining, the accelerator is idle `{python} PipelineCalcs.data_stall_pct_str` of the time. To eliminate the stall entirely, the next batch must arrive within the `{python} PipelineCalcs.t_comp_stall_str` compute window, either by increasing effective storage bandwidth or by adding parallel I/O streams. Deeper prefetch buffers cannot help here, because the delivery time exceeds the compute window on every step, not only in the tail.

:::

The data stall ratio\index{Data stall ratio!diagnostic metric} measures time lost waiting for inputs relative to the chosen iteration window. Acceptable stall time depends on the fleet's cost and throughput objectives; a threshold is a policy choice, not a universal storage-health boundary. Instrument batch-ready times and accelerator execution in the same trace to distinguish input starvation from synchronization, CPU preprocessing, and other idle intervals. General profiling tools can expose these events, but an idle accelerator alone does not identify storage as the cause.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ An I/O-wait efficiency target for the fleet Data axis is operationalized in @sec-appdx-c3-dam-scorecard.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-storage-pipeline-equation monitoring paragraph
# │ Goal: Idle-compute cost of an undetected stall increase on the reference cluster.
# │ How: GPUs x fleet GPU-hour price x one week x stall-ratio increase.
from mlsysim import Systems, Infrastructure
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_usd

class StallMonitoringCost:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    cluster_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_1K.total_accelerators  # 1,024-GPU reference cluster
    gpu_hour_rate = Infrastructure.Pricing.Fleet.GpuHourRef.rate
    week_hours = 168  # one week of wall-clock time
    stall_increase = 0.05  # scenario: undetected stall-ratio increase
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────
    idle_cost = (cluster_gpus * gpu_hour_rate * week_hours * hour * stall_increase).to(USD)
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────
    check(15_000 < idle_cost.magnitude < 20_000, f"Weekly idle cost unexpected: {idle_cost}")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ───────────────────────────────────────
    cluster_gpus_str = fmt(cluster_gpus, precision=0, commas=True)
    gpu_hour_rate_str = fmt_usd(gpu_hour_rate.to(USD / hour).magnitude, precision=0, commas=False, per="GPU-hour")
    idle_cost_usd_str = fmt_usd(idle_cost.magnitude, precision=0)
```

A storage pipeline that met its budget at launch can drift out of it as datasets grow, jobs contend, and drives age, so it requires continuous monitoring to keep silent bottlenecks from eroding training efficiency. Key metrics to track in real time include per-tier bandwidth utilization (NVMe, network, object storage), prefetch buffer depth (how many batches are queued and ready), the data stall ratio per GPU, the parallel file system's metadata operation rate, and NVMe drive health indicators (wear level, temperature, error counts). Alert thresholds should trigger before stalls become visible in training loss curves. An undetected 5 percent increase in data stall ratio across the `{python} StallMonitoringCost.cluster_gpus_str`-GPU reference cluster (half the running cluster) for just one week wastes about `{python} StallMonitoringCost.idle_cost_usd_str` in idle compute\index{Idle compute!economic cost of data stalls} (`{python} StallMonitoringCost.cluster_gpus_str` GPUs $\times$ `{python} StallMonitoringCost.gpu_hour_rate_str` $\times$ 168 hours $\times$ 5 percent), making comprehensive storage monitoring a first-order economic concern rather than an operational nicety.

Diagnose a storage stall at three levels. The application timeline identifies when the accelerator waits; per-worker rates and queue depth identify the pipeline stage that falls behind; device and shared-server counters show which resource limits that stage. Correlating those observations distinguishes a byte-bandwidth shortage from metadata contention or insufficient decoding capacity.

A small development dataset may hide the contention and accumulated state of a production run. A pipeline stress test\index{Pipeline stress test!throughput benchmarking} should therefore use representative data volume and concurrency and run long enough to expose queue depletion, resource leaks, and memory pressure before the loader is coupled to an expensive training job.

Different ML workloads have dramatically different bandwidth profiles, even when using the same cluster. Image classification with ResNet-50\index{ResNet-50!image classification bandwidth} on ImageNet produces a high bandwidth demand because each batch contains hundreds of large images (`{python} PipelineCalcs.img_size_kb_str` each on average) and iteration times are short (100 to 200 ms). Language model pretraining produces a lower per-batch bandwidth demand because tokenized text is compact (each token is a 4-byte integer, so a packed sequence of 4,096 tokens occupies only 16 KB), but the total data volume over the training run is enormous (trillions of tokens). Recommendation model training, the Archetype B (DLRM at Scale) workload, produces a mixed bandwidth demand: embedding lookups require high-IOPS random access to the embedding table, while the dense layers consume standard sequential training data. Each workload's bandwidth profile determines which storage tier is the bottleneck and where optimization effort should focus. Archetype C (Federated MobileNet) falls outside this shared-storage analysis, because its raw training data stays on the devices that produce it; there is no central corpus to stage, and its storage constraints become per-device capacity and upload limits.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ On-device training data and federated updates are developed in @sec-edge-intelligence.
:::

@Fig-data-stall-frontier bounds the compute active-time fraction\index{GPU utilization!storage bandwidth limit} as a function of the bandwidth-to-demand ratio across an ideal overlapped pipeline. Defining input demand as batch bytes divided by uninterrupted compute time, the piecewise curve ramps linearly through bandwidth-starved operating points before flattening at the supply-equals-demand saturation knee (ratio = 1). The active fraction is the smaller of one and available bandwidth divided by that demand, assuming no other bottleneck.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: stall-frontier-points-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ DATA-STALL FRONTIER OPERATING POINTS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-data-stall-frontier and the paragraph that reads its markers.
# │
# │ Goal: Place three of the chapter's worked workloads on the ideal overlapped
# │       frontier, active fraction = min(1, supply / demand).
# │ Show: text job ~6,000x headroom, image job ~3.3x, stall notebook 0.8.
# │ How:  Supply = the 1 TB/s parallel file system (text, image jobs) or the
# │       per-batch delivery rate (notebook); demand from earlier LEGO cells.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent

class StallFrontierPoints:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ─────────────────────────────────────────
    pfs_bw = Systems.Storage.PfsOneTbPerSecond.bandwidth
    text_demand = TextImageBandwidth.text_bw
    image_demand = TextImageBandwidth.image_bw
    t_comp = PipelineCalcs.t_comp
    t_io = PipelineCalcs.t_io

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────
    text_ratio = (pfs_bw / text_demand).to("").magnitude
    image_ratio = (pfs_bw / image_demand).to("").magnitude
    stall_ratio = (t_comp / t_io).to("").magnitude  # delivery rate / consumption rate
    stall_active = min(1.0, stall_ratio)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────
    check(text_ratio > 1000, "Text job should have three orders of magnitude of PFS headroom")
    check(1 < image_ratio < 10, "Image job should sit a few times above the knee")
    check(abs(stall_active - (1 - PipelineCalcs.data_stall_pct_val / 100)) < 1e-9, "Notebook point must match its 20% stall")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ───────────────────────────────────────
    pfs_bw_tb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(pfs_bw, unit=TB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    text_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(text_ratio, -3), precision=0, commas=True)
    image_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(image_ratio, precision=1, commas=False)
    stall_active_pct_str = fmt_percent(stall_active, precision=0, commas=False, style="prose")
```

::: {#fig-data-stall-frontier fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The data-stall frontier**: In the ideal overlapped pipeline, the compute active-time fraction is min(1, available bandwidth / input demand), plotted against a logarithmic bandwidth ratio. Markers place three of the chapter's workloads on the curve: the data-stall notebook's pipeline, whose delivery time exceeds its compute window, and the image and text jobs of the text-versus-image bandwidth comparison, each served by the whole parallel file system. The curve is an ideal service-rate bound, not an empirical utilization curve or a claim about a storage technology." fig-alt="Piecewise curve of compute active-time fraction against bandwidth divided by demand on a log axis, rising to one at the matching point. A marker at 0.8 sits on the rising segment; image and text job markers sit on the flat segment, the text job far to the right."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-data-stall-frontier
# │ Goal: Ideal active-time fraction from overlapped service times, with the
# │       chapter's operating points from StallFrontierPoints.
import numpy as np
from binder.tools.figures import style as book_style

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = book_style.setup_plot(figsize=(8, 4.5))
bandwidth_ratio = np.logspace(-1, 4, 400)
active_fraction = np.minimum(1, bandwidth_ratio)
assert np.all((active_fraction >= 0) & (active_fraction <= 1))
ax.plot(bandwidth_ratio, active_fraction, color=COLORS['BlueLine'], linewidth=2.4, label='Ideal overlapped pipeline')
ax.axvline(1, color=COLORS['OrangeLine'], linestyle='--', linewidth=1.2, label='Supply = demand')
points = [
    # Red marks only the stalled operating point; healthy (fed) jobs are green.
    (StallFrontierPoints.stall_ratio, StallFrontierPoints.stall_active, 'Data-stall notebook', (1.4, 0.42), COLORS['RedLine']),
    (StallFrontierPoints.image_ratio, 1.0, 'Image job, whole PFS', (5.0, 0.72), COLORS['GreenLine']),
    (StallFrontierPoints.text_ratio, 1.0, 'Text job, whole PFS', (250, 0.55), COLORS['GreenLine']),
]
for x, y, label, (tx, ty), color in points:
    ax.plot([x], [y], marker='o', markersize=7, color=color, zorder=5)
    ax.annotate(label, xy=(x, y), xytext=(tx, ty), fontsize=9, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color=color, lw=0.9))
ax.set_xscale('log')
ax.set_xlabel('Available bandwidth / workload input demand')
ax.set_ylabel('Compute active-time fraction')
ax.set_xlim(0.1, 1e4)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.1)
ax.legend(loc='lower right', frameon=True)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
plt.close()
```

:::

Below matching supply, bandwidth increases raise the ideal active fraction proportionally. Above it, more bandwidth does not improve this ideal compute stage, although headroom can help absorb contention and variable delivery. The markers show how far apart the chapter's workloads sit. Served by the whole `{python} StallFrontierPoints.pfs_bw_tb_per_s_str` parallel file system, the text job of notebook \ref{nbk-data-storage-text-vs-image-bandwidth} has about `{python} StallFrontierPoints.text_ratio_mult_str` more bandwidth than it consumes, the image job only `{python} StallFrontierPoints.image_ratio_mult_str`, and the pipeline of notebook \ref{nbk-data-storage-data-stall-ratio} sits left of the knee at `{python} StallFrontierPoints.stall_active_pct_str` active time. Real systems can fall below the curve because of preprocessing, latency tails, or synchronization. The graph identifies a workload service-rate boundary; it does not establish that every job needs every storage tier.

The pipeline equation also reveals a scaling challenge that worsens with cluster size. As $\AcceleratorCountGpu$ increases, the required bandwidth $\Bandwidth_{\text{required}}$ increases linearly, but the storage system's aggregate bandwidth does not automatically scale to match. Adding more compute nodes to a cluster that shares a parallel file system increases the demand on a fixed storage resource. Eventually, the storage system saturates and every additional GPU beyond the saturation point contributes zero additional training throughput while increasing cost. This saturation point is the practical upper limit on cluster scaling for a given storage configuration, and identifying it quantitatively requires applying @eq-pipeline-throughput to the specific storage system's measured bandwidth.

### Pipelining and prefetching {#sec-storage-pipelining}

@Fig-data-pipeline-vol2 contrasts sequential and overlapped execution across concurrent storage, CPU, and GPU timeline lanes, demonstrating how pipelining\index{Pipelining!data loading} shields the accelerator from I/O stalls. Staging and preparing batch $i+1$ on host resources while the GPU trains on batch $i$ hides input work when delivery keeps pace and enough prepared work absorbs latency variation.

::: {#fig-data-pipeline-vol2 fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Pipelined data loading**: Both panels share one time scale, with illustrative stage durations. Sequential loading (a) leaves the GPU idle while each batch is read and prepared. Pipelined loading (b) reads and prepares batch $i+1$ while the GPU trains on batch $i$, so four batches finish in about the time sequential loading needs for two. The overlap hides storage latency only while delivery keeps pace with compute and the prefetch buffer is deep enough to absorb variance." fig-alt="Two timelines with storage, CPU, and GPU lanes on a shared time axis. Panel a: read, prep, and train blocks run one after another for two batches, with dashed idle blocks on the GPU lane. Panel b: four back-to-back reads, four prep blocks, and four back-to-back train blocks after one initial idle block, spanning about the same length as panel a."}
